Sources indicate that episodes: Narrative-driven encounters that create stories inspired by The Simpsons. Episodes play out across seasonal boards, sticker sets, and minigames, all capped off with an animated short.

Sticker sets: Every Episode comes with its own limited-time sticker set, taking cues from the latest Simpsons story. Collectible artwork, character journeys and other rewards are yours to claim for the duration of each Episode.

Simpsons-themed Shutdowns and Heists: Monopoly Go's shutdowns and heists get a Simpsons makeover, with Springfield-inspired chaos and disasters.

Bribe Wiggum: This changes Go to Jail to allow players to bribe Chief Wiggum, giving you a chance to earn a bigger reward, but not without introducing an element of unpredictability.

Simpsons chance cards: The chance card collection grows with over 50 Simpsons-themed cards full of memes, references and one-liners from the show.

According to recent reports, an unofficial GTA 6 PC release is in sight. GTA 6 leaker Cyberleek has released the executable file for the Xbox build of the game, which was shared earlier this month, formally firing the starting shot on recompilation work that could soon see Rockstar's game running on PC.

Sources indicate that users flagged the November 23 release of the Xbox EXE online. "The torch passes to the open source recomp and emulation projects. Before trusting any file, verify it," a message from Cyberleek reads.

According to recent reports, project Leonida is at the forefront of those recompilation efforts, pushing for a native GTA 6 version based on the leaked Xbox build. One of Leonida's lead developers, Shayder, reacted to the executable leak on Twitter: "CL has just dropped the exe, expect a lot of static recompilation work to be done soon.".

Leonida is right now available to access online, with its creators noting it "does not contain the game, keys or an executable, and it does not explain how to get them. You need your own copy, with its files already readable on disk. Nothing here decrypts or works around any protection." You'll be shocked to hear the recomp is co-authored by Claude AI.

The release of this executable has not changed that, but it has kicked the GTA 6 PC race into high gear.

Just hours after the EXE arrived, an update went out to the Leonida Discord server: "The game almost boots. Black screen, audio cuts off.".

After the news broke, the Leonida Discord server buckled under an influx of new people, forcing the moderators to end a live stream amid a temporary outage. The server was "not nuked," states one admin.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more.

The latest Leonida status enhancement reads: "Everything that can be done without the game's executable is in place, so work on booting can start as soon as one is available to a developer." Development is moving fast with that keystone now in place, though the game remains unplayable on PC.

An official GTA 6 PC version is expected to be released in the next year or two at the latest, following Rockstar's pattern with titles like GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2.

Previously, CEO Strauss Zelnick of Rockstar owner Take-Two Interactive mentioned GTA 6 being pirated is just "a fact of life," though he also said the organization has its legal team on standby to handle any problems. I wonder how they'd react to a playable PC build surfacing, presently, less than one week after GTA 6's console launch.

GTA 6's Lucia is "long overdue," OG Grand Theft Auto lead says – because Rockstar's representation of women "has not been good".

  • Worst Class Ever is a upcoming don't-call-it-friendslop asymmetrical multiplayer game dedicated to such larks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, what's the best prank you ever pulled on a teacher in school, assuming you went to school? By which I mean, a genuinely funny prank that didn't cause any injuries, break any of the more key laws (legal or ethical), or leave anybody with years of mental distress.

In a recent development, I'll start: I once had to write a four-page punishment essay with the topic "silence is golden", after being caught talking in class. I took the essay very seriously for the first three pages, only to end it with the phrase "...but not as golden as my arse." The teacher who set me the essay smugly tore it up without reading it - as I knew he would. Checkmate, Mr Thompson. Decades later, the last laugh remains mine.

Worst Class Ever is a upcoming don't-call-it-friendslop asymmetrical multiplayer game dedicated to such larks. One player is a teacher, and seven others are naughty delinquent children, hiding in amongst some well-brought-up and obedient NPCs. As the wayward tykes, your goal is to do mischievous things like eating at your desk, passing notes, dropping banana skins, and playing on your phone, without being spotted by Teach.

All of this takes place in a breezy modern Japanese high school, the kind familiar from a million animes. Bagsy the Protagonist Desk by the window at the back of the class! The maplist spans the curriculum, from computer labs to gym tracks to stepped lecture theatres. I don't think there are any covert edu-tainment mechanics, but if you're playing Teacher, I guess there's nothing to stop you actually explaining the periodic table while trying to work out who keeps throwing chalk at your head.

What a wholesome and whimsical place! Such happy memories! Oh crikey, the male teacher is terrifying – why can't he stop grinning? And why do I have a smoke grenade? Why is this lesson taking place in the dark? Why are the teachers permitted to punch the students and tie them to wooden posts? Worst Class Ever definitely isn't a horror game, but I'm not sure I'd send my kids to this particular institution. I feel like we're one texture pack away from playing a more sociable version of Little Nightmares. Read more on Steam.

#166348. Five Things I Wish I'd Known Before Getting a Foldable Phone

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1350 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Five Things I Wish I'd Known Before Getting a Foldable Phone

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1350 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The iPhone Duo might be the highest profile foldable phone to date, but it’s by no means the first.
  • One of the most notable aspects of the iPhone Duo is how wide its screen is, even while closed.
  • Compare with my Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which features an extremely tall 2.17:1 aspect ratio when closed, but a nearly square 1:04:1 aspect ratio when open.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The iPhone Duo might be the highest profile foldable phone to date, but it’s by no means the first. Personally, I’ve had my eye on the Google variant, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold—and recently I finally took the plunge. I thought I’d done my research to know how different having a foldable phone would be, but I still had a bit to learn. Here are some of the things I wish I’ve learned along the way after making the jump to foldables.

One of the most notable aspects of the iPhone Duo is how wide its screen is, even while closed. And there’s a good reason for that: The larger screen while open has exactly the same 1.41:1 aspect ratio as the smaller screen while closed. This has a ripple effect on how every app you use looks and feels—and whether you like Apple’s approach is largely a matter of personal preference.

Compare with my Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which features an extremely tall 2.17:1 aspect ratio when closed, but a nearly square 1:04:1 aspect ratio when open. On the outer screen, apps are a little less wide than on my old phone, but there’s plenty of space for reading books or articles on the inner screen.

In a recent development, I like the tall, thin display personally because it feels easier to reach buttons with my thumb, and the wider display is better for reading. However, this approach can occasionally result in some odd app layouts. Not every app is designed for tablets, especially on Android, and shifting the aspect ratio between the inner and outer display sometimes means re-rendering or even restarting an app entirely to load properly.

Sources indicate that the iPhone Duo has a more consistent aspect ratio and general feel between the inner and outer display, but it comes at the cost of a really wide phone. Neither approach is better or worse on its own, but it might be worth going to a local store to get your hands on the phone you’re thinking about before buying.

According to recent reports, for years, the screens on most smartphones have been made of increasingly tough and scratch-resistant glass. So tough that you might not even need a screen protector anymore. On a foldable phone, that can be true of the outside display, but it’s very much not when it comes to the inner, foldable display.

Sources indicate that screens might be foldable, but the strong, durable glass that makes your phone so scratch-resistant isn’t. No matter what foldable phone you use, the covering on the inner display will be more flexible, and thus softer. Apple uses a nano-texture polymer film that can be replaced, but the film on most foldable phones cannot. That means if they get damaged or scratched, those marks will be there for the life of your phone.

If you (like me) haven’t considered a screen protector in a while, it might be time to try one again, at least for the inner display. It’s also worth keeping in mind how rough you plan to be with your phone. Construction sites or factories might not be the best home for a foldable phone you plan to open a lot, but an office job should be a bit safer.

It has been revealed that similar to the screen protector issue, cases can be more of a headache. Most rigid cases will come in two pieces, and the piece that covers the outer display can be shockingly minimal—barely more than a frame, for some of the cases I looked at. A poorly made case can be brittle or pop off more easily, so it’s more notable to get a high-quality one.

In a recent development, if you like to use your phone case as your wallet, it’s also important to be wary of cases that aren’t specifically designed for your model of phone (and maybe some that are). A lot of wallet cases are built to unfold to reveal your phone’s screen on one side, and your cards and ID on the other. But depending on how your foldable phone unfolds, it could be awkward to reach the inner screen.

Industry observers note that the hinge also introduces more spaces for dust and debris to get into your phone. Despite the extra moving parts and gaps, most foldable phones still offer the now-standard IP68 dust and water resistance rating. That mainly applies to what can get inside and damage the components inside your phone. It’s still possible for hair and dirt to get gummed up in any pinchable spaces, so look out for any case that might provide even more nooks for dust to collect in.

Sources indicate that I’ve set up most of my apps how I like them by now, but when I first got my foldable phone, I had to revisit some settings I thought I was done messing with. One of the most notable examples was my ebook apps: I was previously using a single-column, medium-font layout, but it looked ridiculous on the inner display. After switching to a two-column layout, it not only felt more natural, but a lot like reading a regular book.

Similarly, there were some uses for my calendar app that got a whole lot more useful. I’ve never really been able to use anything other than either the one-day or Schedule view if I want to make out anything, but on the inner screen, I can finally look at my week at a glance. But that meant tweaking some things—like showing reminders, which fit naturally amid my events in Schedule view, but become a cluttered mess when I saw 14 different reminders to take my meds at once in the Week view.

Sources indicate that most apps do a decent job of automatically adjusting to different screen sizes, but I found a few outliers that I had to figure out myself. As an example, Google Docs would default to a view with extremely tiny text when I first started using it. It took me a bit to figure out that this was due to a “Print layout” toggle in the document’s settings. This is, for some reason, enabled by default when opening a document on the larger inner screen. It can take some time to learn the eccentricities of all your apps, but it’s worth poking around when you can.

I know, it sounds so obvious, right? The outer screen is the one you’ll use most often, so how could you forget about it? But when you unfold the inner screen, the outer one is still useful in some surprising ways that I hadn’t even considered until I went poking around in some of my apps.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most adorable examples is the Made You Look feature in the Pixel’s Camera app. When unfolded, you can take a picture using the rear camera and see a preview like normal, while the outer screen shows silly animations to capture the attention of a baby or toddler that you want to look into the camera. Admittedly, this is an older feature, but it’s a clever one. For adults, you can also use the outer display to get a selfie preview while using the rear-facing camera.

Industry observers note that the outer screen is also just better for some things. YouTube is one of the few apps that has a unique layout designed for a partially folded screen, with the video playing on the tilted-up portion of the screen, and video controls on the bottom portion.

Industry observers note that however, in my experience, it was a lot nicer to watch a YouTube video by just propping up the outer screen by unfolding the phone a bit, like a kickstand. My Pixel even detected when YouTube was in full-screen mode on the outer display and would be more forgiving of unfolding the phone without switching to the inner screen. The phone anticipated I might just want to prop up the smaller screen, which I thought was a nice touch.

Breaking: While soulslikes went bigger than significant, Death's Door swung open the appeal of a tighter adventure

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (557 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Declaring a Best Way of Doing Things is a fool’s game, though in recent years my favourite entries in the Tricky Hitting genre – inclusive of soulslikes and their hybridised disciples – have been the big, bulging ones.
  • Industry observers note that even in the latter stages, with a full kit of precisely four ranged spells, Death’s Door is a simple proposition.
  • Still, it’s clever with its limitations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Declaring a Best Way of Doing Things is a fool’s game, though in recent years my favourite entries in the Tricky Hitting genre – inclusive of soulslikes and their hybridised disciples – have been the big, bulging ones. Elden Rings and Silksongs, with vast kingdoms and deep, rattling toolkits for surviving them. The reason it’s a fool’s game is because you can also have something like Death’s Door, a taut, compact, lighthearted little actioner that fills eight hours instead of 80 and yet never feels underwhelming or compromised for it.

Industry observers note that even in the latter stages, with a full kit of precisely four ranged spells, Death’s Door is a simple proposition. You are a crow. You hit things. Occasionally you shoot things. You collect the souls of a frog, a yeti, and a grandmother. Everything in-between directly relates to finding the errant monster/pensioner, or at a stretch, upgrading one of those four abilities.

Still, it’s clever with its limitations. Environments are small in number but vary wildly in tone and texture, and they tightly weave their paths into criss-crossing bundles that maximise travel – evoking the sense of a great, ranging adventure within relatively tiny spaces. The lack of a wiki’s worth of combat options also never becomes a problem, partly because it spreads out its spell unlocks, and partly because the smooth, flowing back-and-forths of its central swordplay are pleasurable enough to carry it anyway. Good bosses, too! They’re all characterful, memorable weirdoes who fight unlike anyone in their minion armies, and usually come with a hidden weakness to deduce and exploit.

It has been revealed that which is welcome, as these major lads and lasses do tend to launch difficulty spikes right up your feathered backside, and do so in a game that isn’t otherwise as fussed about trial-and-error pain endurance as some of its inspirations. They don’t, however, bring the mood down. At times, this tale of a pitch-black soul reaper working as an agent of Death (complete with an office of Death and embittered co-workers of Death) can get downright cosy, leading through you through warmly-lit jungles and breezy waterside ruins.

Recently replaying, I’d also forgotten how witty it can be. Little gaglets are sprinkled throughout, both visual and verbal, but the best jokes are saved for – funnily enough – the bosses, who’ll raise your pre-fight spirit with some amusingly terrible trash talk before becoming the punchline themselves. I audibly wheezed the first time a death animation immediately cut to the foe’s impromptu funeral, their beaked killer among the precious few guests. And even when the joke is recycled later, I couldn’t help tittering at the sight of my enemy – who seconds earlier, had been attempting to fatally sit on me – lying nobly in state.

I previously considered ending my Valor Mortis review by calling it a gateway into the more demanding side of action-RPGs; a shorter, simpler alternative to FromSoft’s overwhelming titans that might nonetheless serve to introduce curious newcomers to their shared quirks and qualities. The game equivalent of splashing your chest with water before jumping into a pool. In hindsight, Death’s Door was always a better fit for that description, though there’s enough else here you don’t need to be prepping for something tougher to appreciate its lean, keen adventuring.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, by using auto drive in GTA 6 you get the opportunity to appreciate the level of detail your vehicle has, and how beautiful the world is around you, without the risk of slamming straight into the back of the next car as soon as you hit traffic. When you're not dealing with the controls yourself it can be quite relaxing to cruise around GTA 6, soaking up the sights and generally admiring everything Rockstar has created. To find out how it all works, here's how to enable auto drive in GTA 6.

In a recent development, to use GTA 6 auto drive, you need to be in control of a vehicle and have a destination marker set on your map. From the vehicle, hold Down on the D-pad to access the camera options, then while still holding it press Options (PS5) or Menu (Xbox) to enter the CINEMATIC menu. You'll then see a prompt for ENABLE AUTO DRIVE in the bottom right corner, so hold the appropriate button to get it started.

According to recent reports, jason or Lucia will then begin driving on their own towards the destination, as the camera cycles through various cinematic views. You can use the right stick to move the camera around, and click R3/RS to switch to the next view. The triggers will also let you choose between three driving speeds, to determine how fast your driver will go, and you can change the destination marker on the map at any time to reroute.

We need to be clear that this is certainly not fast travel in GTA 6, as Jason or Lucia will obey all road rules and spend a lot of time sat in traffic, so it is instead intended as a way to soak up the atmosphere and get some great video footage or screenshots of your journey.

It has been revealed that also, be aware that auto drive in GTA 6 doesn't make everything perfect, and when I used it another driver hit my car then got out and started attacking it with a wrench! If something similar happens to you, then here's how to repair and fix your car in GTA 6.

Sources indicate that mucky and disreputable kiosk game Probably Stolen – Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim is getting three substantial updates over the next few months that add extra starting scenarios, building on the existing wealth of goods, materials, vocations and techs. Those starting scenarios range from peddling human meat to running the finest cyber-frappucino stall this side of Tannhäuser Gate. There are no hard release dates, and the contents of each patch may alter, but developers Questing Goose Studio have shared some rough timeframes.

Recent findings suggest that coming up in mid-December, there's the Junker starting scenario, which I assume is all about trading scrap, rather than being a Prussian nobleman. You'll get a bespoke perk, fresh items, and the ability to hire, equip and send scavs on expeditions. This update will also include some minor expansions for the Fence and Gunsmith vocations – the latter will be able to flog or otherwise make use of shotgun shells, 25mm grenade rounds and a tier 3 handmade SMG, alongside new armour.

Sources indicate that late January is when you'll "very likely" get the chance to be an Organ Dealer, care of the second major patch. "Players will start by buying different organs and fulfilling specific requests, and will later be able to grow or print organs," a Steam blog explains. You'll also be able to filter blood and remove diseases, with different blood types having different value modifiers. How will you get your hands on organs? By sending horrible black market thugs on foraging "expeditions".

Recent findings suggest that last but not least, the planned April update will add the Street Food Vendor starting scenario. This lets you weave a livelihood around choice beverages and edibles from a range of cultures, supported by updates to the game's Aquaculture and Hydroponics tech. Sounds a lot cheerier than the organ trading racket, but then again, Probably Stolen will doubtless find a way to make it utterly grim. Guests at Sweeney's Cantina know better than to ask what our frappucinos are made of.

Recent findings suggest that are you playing Probably Stolen? It's been doing better than expected. I was keen on the demo, but my attention was lured away by a truly upsetting game about dogpeople in caves.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the BF Bandito is one of the many cars in GTA 6 that Moses asks you to steal and bring to him for cold, hard cash. This one has a search area out in Buskin Swamp, but when you arrive it's not immediately clear where or how to steal the car.

The owner of this white offroad racer will drive around the map marked search area in a circle, as shown in the clip above. To get him to stop, simply park your car blocking the track and stand next to it. When he reaches you, he'll slow down and call out, at which point you should press L2 to focus on him and use the "Mislead" dialogue option to ask for help.

In a recent development, in my version, Lucia was wearing a ski-mask and had a baseball bat, which swiftly convinced them all to run away (after a few swings), but either way, once he stops it's easy to steal the car. The baseball bat probably wasn't necessary, but hey, it's still non-lethal.

As you exit the swamp, you'll get shot at and pursued by a few of his friends, but the BF Bandito is fast enough to outrun them easily. Bring it back to Moses to get $3,400ish as reward, though this may vary based on condition.

First-person psychological horror game BrokenLore: DON’T PLAY will launch for Switch 2 alongside its previously unveiled PlayStation 5, Xbox Series, and PC (Steam, Epic Games Store) versions, Serafini Productions announced.

Here is an overview of the game, via Serafini Productions:.

BrokenLore: DON’T PLAY is a first-person psychological horror game that follows Hideo, a young hikikomori obsessed with video games and the need for recognition. When he receives a mysterious experimental console in the mail, he decides to play it, convinced it could change his life.

Sources indicate that but each level brings increasingly unsettling consequences into the real world. His apartment begins to shift, time starts to distort, and something dark slowly emerges as the line between what he plays and what he lives begins to break down.

Across five levels that draw Hideo deeper into his obsession, BrokenLore: DON’T PLAY takes him on a disturbing psychological descent, exploring themes of alienation, the need for validation, and identity loss.

In this upcoming installment, players will once again encounter familiar characters:.

It has been revealed that brokenLore: DON’T PLAY is part of the BrokenLore saga, a psychological horror anthology where each game stands on its own, yet hides fragments of a deeper truth. Through secrets, environments, and hidden details, every chapter reveals pieces of an unseen narrative, slowly forming the larger mystery known as Elysium.

  • In a recent development, in any case, the update goes a tad further than that.

A massive part of the point of The Blood of Dawnwalker is that you're on a fixed time limit. You've got 30 in-game days and nights to try and save your family, and if you don't manage to see everything the game has to offer, well, the game's director is fine with that. But that doesn't matter as much now, as The Blood of Dawnwalker is getting its 1.2 enhancement next week that adds in a fresh game plus mode.

Recent findings suggest that "If you completed the Epilogue, you can dive right back into Vale Sangora with New Game+!" a post from the devs explains. "Your level, skills, and inventory will carry over; the level cap will be raised to 100; enemies will be balanced and scale uniformly across all regions; and items will have NG+ versions with updated stats." Sounds like your usual new game plus affair! I suppose it is a good opportunity to try out different things compared to your first playthrough, but I'm not exactly aligned with the idea that the timer restriction is too restricting (as some mods have made clear how others feel that way).

In a recent development, in any case, the update goes a tad further than that. If you got the Eclipse Edition of the game, the in-game soundtrack that came with it "will be extended with additional songs from the game." You can expect the soundtrack on streaming services soon, too. While details are slimmer here, there are also some planned balance changes, like updated enemy health pools and how often they use their abilities during combat, and terrain geometry has seen some improvements to allow for "smoother movement during combat and exploration.".

According to recent reports, overall, a bit of a smaller revision compared to the last one, but one I'm sure will be welcome to some all the same. If you've not had a chance to check the game out yet and still feel on the fence about it, here's some lovely words from Mark's review: "There’s always that sense that something important or unexpected could be lurking around the next corner, to pull you into a quest dripping with depth and intrigue. It works to ensure the more busywork-esque tasks attached to angering Brencis and his Boyars never make Vale Sangora feel home to a string of boring boxes to tick. It’s a vibrant, constantly changing place with a thousand different threads metaphorically criss-crossing just beneath its surface, just as ancient ruins literally criss-cross beneath its swamps, crags, and forests.".

Industry observers note that earlier this year in a bit of a shakeup for the fleshiest kid in town, Super Meat Boy entered into a newly introduced dimension in the aptly named Super Meat Boy 3D. I've not played it but it seems like a good take on the format. Clearly, though, sometimes you just need to play the hits, as a new release of the original game is on the way in the form of Super Meat Boy Again+, a remaster with updated graphics, levels and plenty more.

According to recent reports, what is there is very clearly Super Meat Boy, uh, again, just with a major new lick of paint. There is probably some kind of joke to be made about it being DLSS yassified, but I'm too tired to think of one, so, you get the point. But it does look pretty good! I do kind of miss the Flash game aesthetic, I think there's a real charm to the sort of visual design sensibilities you'd find from that era, but this remaster certainly ain't ugly at least. Apparently it's not just the art that's new, as there's also new music, cutscenes, secrets and "stuff.".

If the animated sequences featured in the trailer, which you can have a gander at above, are included in the final game that'll be a treat to watch too, as I think they better capture the Newgrounds pseudo sub-genre of animation than the graphical overhaul. It sounds like they will be looking at the Steam page, so, a treat to look forward to while committing an act of masochism by playing it!

It has been revealed that there's no release date attached to this remaster, so we'll all just have to sit tight for an update there. The original is still listed on Steam, but if you fancy as big a dose of nostalgia as the trailer is trying to present to you, you could always go play the original, plain old regular Meat Boy. It's playable right on Newgrounds thanks to the Flash emulator Ruffle and works like a dream! Or if you're happy to wait, you could always wishlist the latest one on Steam.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When you think about GTA as a series, the first thing that probably comes to mind is driving through crowds of people, gunning down whoever you like, just generally doing crime without any care in the world.
  • "Crime is a fundamental part of GTA - at least up until now, it has been," Nelson told The Guardian (via @GameRoll_, ta IGN) in a latest interview.
  • I am deeply curious as to what those mechanics may be, given that most of what we've seen so far is pretty relegated to shootin', lootin' and a bit of smoochin'.

When you think about GTA as a series, the first thing that probably comes to mind is driving through crowds of people, gunning down whoever you like, just generally doing crime without any care in the world. I wouldn't exactly call it an empathy game, not to say that other games are any better at such a thing anyway. But with GTA 6 out, crikey, next bloody week, a newly introduced interview has gone up with co-studio head Rob Nelson where he shared that you have a bit more space to be empathetic compared to previous entries.

"Crime is a fundamental part of GTA - at least up until now, it has been," Nelson told The Guardian (via @GameRoll_, ta IGN) in a latest interview. "We're trying to make sure we're not punishing people for playing the game they are used to … [but] your actions will have some effect on how the game plays out." When asked about whether this will be the first GTA game to encourage people to be empathetic, Nelson responded, "I would say so. I would say that it's a product of the story we're trying to tell. We've tried for the first time in a GTA to provide mechanisms that encourage it, for those who want to.".

I am deeply curious as to what those mechanics may be, given that most of what we've seen so far is pretty relegated to shootin', lootin' and a bit of smoochin'. If you steal a car, is there an NPC that loses their job because of it? Can you repair the harm you caused through that action? I'm sure hardly anyone else that's vibrating through their skin in excitement for almost having the game in their fingertips will be asking such questions, I'm just often wary of empathy mechanics in games.

In a recent development, in any case, doesn't matter all that much for us PC lot just yet, especially because Rockstar are preparing themselves both legally and technically to tackle pirated copies of the game. Rockstar will obviously be quite busy at the moment too, not just because of that whole launching a game thing, but because UK-based workers will be voting to unionise as we speak. If formed, it could be 1600 members strong, which would make it the biggest games union in the UK. Solidarity with all the workers as the voting process continues. I hope you get the result you deserve.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when Bethesda got its hands on the Fallout licence way back in 2004, the naysayers were many and vocal. In fairness, the naysayers are still many and vocal, but they were back then too, and it turns out Bethesda saw at least a few of their posts. In a chat with The Examined Game, Skyrim lead Bruce Nesmith reflected on the reaction some Fallout old-heads had to Bethesda's acquisition of the series.

Industry observers note that "There was huge pushback when Bethesda got the Fallout licence to do Fallout 3. There was a lot of people who were Obsidian fans, who were like 'Bethesda's gonna screw it up, they're just gonna make it Skyrim, we want Fallout the way we remember Fallout', and there was a strong, vocal community that just hated that we were gonna make that game".

For clarity's sake, the angry fans at the time were likely Black Isle and Interplay fans rather than Obsidian fans—the latter studio hadn't ever made a Fallout game in 2004 (though it had Fallout alumni on staff), and they were prophesying (after 2006) that Bethesda's take on Fallout would be like Oblivion, not Skyrim, since the latter released in 2011. I suspect Nesmith is muddling the initial negative reaction with, well, the more modern one, which is shaped in large part by Obsidian's excellent Fallout: Upcoming Vegas from 2010.

Recent findings suggest that "We had to prove them wrong", recalls Nesmith, "and fortunately we did, because Fallout 3 was embraced even by a lot of our sceptics". It's true: people bloody loved Fallout 3 and still do, though there are of course still series fans who reject the game. "There's always going to be some diehard people that say 'Fallout 2 was the greatest Fallout game ever', but we tried our best to just not engage… because you're not going to win that argument.

Industry observers note that "All you can do is make the best game you can and let that be your statement. And that's what Bethesda did".

It has been revealed that does the vitriol ever get to Bethesda and its devs? Unsurprisingly, yeah, a little. "Any time somebody indicates that the thing you're doing is, you know, fill in your blank for all the cuss words and the bad things… you feel like it's a statement about yourself. You have to divorce yourself from that [but] you can't help but take it a little bit personally. But it does make you want to prove them wrong. It does make you want to say 'I'm going to show you that this will work, that we can respect the franchise and make it better and make it our way, rather than the old way".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The knightly Bretonnia faction is getting a major refresh in Warhammer The Old World, and they're every bit as impressive as you'd hope from such a regal army.

In an update to the old range that has been kicking around for well over a decade, we're now getting fully remodeled Bretonnia Knights of the Realm on horseback – which can also be made as the junior Knights Errant – alongside brand-upcoming Pegasus Knights. It's unclear when the models will launch (there's no chance of them appearing in this week's Black Friday Warhammer deals, so forget about that), but we do know they'll be available first in an Army Reinforcement box set.

In a recent development, latest to The Old World? The best place to start is the 2026 Core Set, which provides everything you need to play: rules, dice, a battlemat, and two small armies. It's tricky to get hold of in the US right now (though I did find some stock at Amazon), but it's available at a discount in the UK via indie stores like Zatu.

Considering how we got a revamp of the skeletal Tomb Kings of Khemri recently, it makes sense that the Bretonnians would follow. These two factions were the first to be launched for Old World, after all. You can get a closer look via Warhammer Community's official reveal, but suffice to say they're utterly gorgeous – especially when lined up in serried ranks.

However, I'm most interested in what these models represent. Their existence after a string of major additions (those new Tomb Kings units, an entirely fresh range of Chaos models, and the Grand Army of Cathay) indicates just how seriously Warhammer takes The Old World – and presumably how popular it's been, considering the way it keeps receiving such generous updates. I can only imagine how costly such a major overhaul has to be, so getting one after another tells you a lot about the Old World's general health.

Seeing as The Old World's predecessor (Warhammer Fantasy Battles) was scrapped in favor of the smaller and lighter Age of Sigmar back in 2015, I'd say that's one hell of a comeback.

While we're talking fantasy, fans adore this Lord of the Rings card game, and it's probably one of the best on Middle-earth.

I've been writing about games in one form or another since 2012, but these days you'll find me managing GamesRadar+'s tabletop gaming and toy coverage (I spend my time here handling everything from board game reviews to the latest Lego news). I've also been obsessed with Warhammer since the 1990s, and love nothing more than running tabletop RPGs like D&D as a Dungeon Master.

Tech Report: Rasen, out in early access now, is a PvP focused take on Dark Souls that borrows one of fighting games' best techy tricks

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the idea of Dark Souls PvP has always scared me a tad.
  • Recent findings suggest that to say that it is just straight up Dark Souls combat would be unfair, from the looks of things.
  • You can take part in matches with up to eight people, which presumably extends to AI (not that kind) enemies too, in "atmospheric duels, clashes, deathmatches and more." It looks neat!

In a recent development, the idea of Dark Souls PvP has always scared me a tad. You can replace Dark Souls with Bloodborne or Elden Ring, I've typically just been a coward when it comes to the idea of fighting another, real person. They're probably going to be better than me! I don't use tactics in Souls games, I use brute force until I get my way! That being said, I do have to admit I quite like the look of Rasen, a game that is essentially just the PvP component of Dark Souls (or PvE if you just want to take on some computer-controlled enemies) that just launched into early access.

Recent findings suggest that to say that it is just straight up Dark Souls combat would be unfair, from the looks of things. For one, it looks more like it leans a tad towards Sekiro with a blades-only kind of affair, whether that be big or small. And blades a plenty they have, ranging from your classic sword, to scythes, to halberds and all sorts. It's a much flashier looking affair too, with fancy slashing effects that seem to buff moves and a pace that seems much faster than Souls games tend to be.

You can take part in matches with up to eight people, which presumably extends to AI (not that kind) enemies too, in "atmospheric duels, clashes, deathmatches and more." It looks neat! And best of all, unusually for a 3D arena fighter, it has rollback netcode. For those unfamiliar, and to try and explain it simply, this is essentially a bit of tech you'll find in predominantly 2D fighting games that predicts every possible input you could make in a given moment, helping to reduce lag time and allow for tighter matches (and less rage quitting).

That's a bit harder to do in a 3D environment given that you have a lot more options at your disposal when it comes to movement, so if it works that's some impressive stuff! And we could all quite easily find out together, as a demo for Rasen is available to try out. Or, alternatively, you can just pick it up whole hog on Steam right now, as it's available in early access.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if a game is about cooking, at minimum I'll have to give it a quick testspin.
  • Sources indicate that first up, I just have to gush over the artstyle a bit.
  • It has been revealed that I'm also quite pleased about two points made on the game's Steam page.

In a recent development, if a game is about cooking, at minimum I'll have to give it a quick testspin. Outside of this whole writing about video games thing, my other lot in life is soul bound to food, so I'm always curious to see how the two can be mixed together. And earlier this week, The Snackbar at the End of the World was revealed, a wonderfully cartoonish action-adventure game set in a magical, slightly post-apocalyptic version of 1960s Italy where you go out and forage for ingredients while fending off monstrous crops before turning them into tasty meals back in your struggling restaurant.

Sources indicate that first up, I just have to gush over the artstyle a bit. The whole game is hand-drawn with a colourful, comic book look that has an impressive sense of depth to it. It gives off a deep love of Italian architecture and landscapes, and that admiration clearly extends to the food too. Once you've gotten the ingredients you need, you then, loosely in the vein of Cooking Mama, prepare them and make various classic Italian dishes by performing some quick minigames. Simple, but charming! The rest of the time you're off killing some ghoulies that look like mutated fruit and veggies, with the occasional fungus-possessed hog and, uh, haunted statues? I think?

It has been revealed that I'm also quite pleased about two points made on the game's Steam page. First is the content description: "This game features cartoon violence, sensitive political themes set in a fictional world, and depictions of an oppressive government committing crimes against its citizens." There is clearly a romantic quality to the game and I'd be worried if it didn't acknowledge any of the political context of the decades preceding.

Sources indicate that the other line reads, "Every sound effect, musical note, design decision, and line of code is human-made. Because this game is about human relationships and delicious food – and that’s not a story we would ever trust AI to tell." Thank the lord! Right now there's no release date attached to The Snackbar at the End of the World, unsurprising given it was only announced this week. But while we all wait for a date, you could perhaps join me in throwing it a wishlist on Steam.

Ubisoft is reportedly working on a fresh Rainbow Six Vegas game 18 years after the last entry in the series.

Industry observers note that according to Insider Gaming, the project is in early development at Ubisoft Montreal under the codename Spades. It’s one of three fresh projects reportedly in production at the studio, and sources suggest a second of those is also set in the Rainbow Six universe. Eurogamer hasn’t been able to verify the report.

It has been revealed that it’s not yet clear what form the fresh game will take, but Insider Gaming’s sources mentioned it's "likely Vegas 3 rather than a remake" of an existing game. Insider Gaming expects it will be several years before Ubisoft officially reveals a new Vegas game.

Rainbow Six Vegas debuted in 2006, followed by Rainbow Six Vegas 2 in 2008. Since then, the series has centred on 2015's Rainbow Six Siege, and in August, Ubisoft declared Rainbow Six Tactics, a single-player, turn-based spin-off from Ubisoft Paris due in 2027.

Rainbow Six now sits under Vantage Studios, the Ubisoft subsidiary set up last year that also oversees Assassin’s Creed and Far Cry, and in which Tencent holds a 26.32 percent stake.

Last week, we learned that Ubisoft is reportedly working on two new Assassin's Creed games: one set in ancient Rome, and a mobile spin-off set in Jerusalem. The leak came less than a week after Ubisoft issued a statement about the future of the Assassin's Creed series, insisting there are at the moment no new remakes of the series' past games in the works.

Panache Digital Games will release the first major content update for the Early Access version of dark third-person narrative action adventure game 1666: Amsterdam in December, the developer announced. It will expand the game’s world, story, and supernatural abilities.

The December upgrade marks the first major expansion of the Early Access experience, bringing upcoming areas to explore, new supernatural abilities, and another Original for players to confront.

A Newly introduced Region, a New Original, and More Witchcraft.

Arriving during the final moon of the year, the first major revision marks the beginning of a series of planned expansions for 1666: Amsterdam.

Alongside this new location comes another Esbat and a new Original, bringing the next chapter of Noa’s journey to Early Access.

The update will also introduce additional Lux and Nux spells and combos, along with newly introduced jewels and potions, giving players more ways to develop their abilities and approach encounters.

Panache Digital Games will share more details about these additions in the weeks leading up to the December release.

■ Early Access Price Remains Unchanged.

Panache Digital Games has also confirmed that 1666: Amsterdam will remain at its current Early Access price when the December upgrade introduces, with no price increase for the upcoming content.

This first major update is part of the team’s ongoing Early Access roadmap, with further expansions planned as development continues.

1666: Amsterdam is available now in Early Access for PC via Steam and Epic Games Store.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that deciding whether to proceed or postpone the Protective Custody story mission is a significant choice you'll need to make in GTA 6. The mission appears on your map as "Meet Abe" in Chapter 5, once you've completed the mission Operation Savage Glory.

Sources indicate that once you get to Abe's office, Jason will warn Lucia that everything will change after this mission. Lucia will hesitate at the door as you make your choice to "Proceed" or "Postpone.".

In a recent development, this is a pretty big decision, because Protective Custody kicks off the final mission of the game which takes about an hour to play. And even though it's a binary choice between "Proceed" (which starts the mission) and "Postpone" (which delays the mission)" there's actually a third possible outcome based on when you make the choice.

Industry observers note that it's a long mission that will take about an hour to play, so be prepared. You can't save during this mission so make sure you've got the time! Once you've completed the final mission, you can watch the credits and return to the open world so you can continue playing.

You will go back to the open world to continue playing. The "Meet Abe" icon will remain on your map so you can begin the final mission at any point from then on.

There are multiple endings to GTA 6, and I won't spoil them here. But one of the endings is only possible if you postpone the Protective Custody mission until you've deposited $2 million into your Buck Me savings account. That's why when you choose to proceed with the final mission makes a difference.

In a recent development, it's also worth noting (again, without spoilers) that just because you do have $2 million in your Buck Me savings account does not guarantee you will see this particular ending. There are still choices you'll need to make in the final mission that determine which ending you see.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Premier League’s Key Match Incidents (KMI) Panel has adjudged that Liverpool had a penalty wrongly given against them in a recent fixture.

The Reds won their last game before the international break, beating Crystal Palace 3-1 at Selhurst Park, although Alisson Becker was denied a clean sheet by a stoppage-time spot kick awarded to the home side and converted by Eddie Nketiah.

The penalty was awarded for what referee Tony Harrington deemed to be a foul by Milos Kerkez on Dario Osorio when the two players unfortunately clashed heads, and Andoni Iraola noted afterwards that he was ‘very upset‘ over that decision.

The Premier League’s KMI Panel has now published its findings from the most recent top-flight matchday (via premierleague.com), and all five independent assessors adjudged that the penalty award against Liverpool was incorrect.

However, there was also unanimous agreement that VAR was right not to intervene, as it was decreed that no ‘clear and obvious’ error had taken place.

The panel concluded: ‘The panel unanimously felt that the referee’s call of a penalty for a challenge by Kerkez on Osorio was incorrect, with the contact being inevitable given the jumping actions of both players.

‘However, the non-intervention of VAR was supported on the basis it was not a clear and obvious error.’.

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

Liverpool fans must be getting sick of hearing from the Premier League’s KMI Panel at this stage, with this incident coming fresh off the back of the panel ruling that we should’ve had a penalty for Jurrien Timber’s blatant shirt pull on Alexander Isak in the 0-1 defeat to Arsenal.

In a recent development, the incident with Kerkez and Osorio wasn’t as black-and-white, but the decision to award a spot kick still felt rather curious at the time. Luckily for Harrington, it came too late to have any major bearing on the overall result at Selhurst Park.

Still, to hear that an independent panel unanimously acknowledged that the Reds were wronged by another refereeing error is galling for everyone associated with LFC, and yet again it calls into question the standads of officiating in the Premier League.

It’s the kind of inconsistency between Kerkez having a spot kick given against him for a 50/50 duel, and Timber getting away with a blatant infringement, which drives players, coaches, fans and pundits absolutely berserk.

Thankfully the decision in the Palace game didn’t do any lasting harm for Liverpool, but you get the sense that it won’t be long before another contentious decision goes against us and the KPI Panel is wheeled out to tell us what we can already deduce for ourselves.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that while following a peculiar trail of silver and saffron leaves around the largest roots of the Treehouse, you come across a hexagonal wooden door lying half-hidden among ivy and moss. Scraping away the dirt, you discover a faint, absurd engraving of a newspaper. What mystery is here? You turn the brass knob – strange, it is warm! – and the engraving of the newspaper flutters. The pages turn faster and faster, emitting a howling gale that bowls you head over foot. When you pick yourself up, you are inside a vast attic full of books and bricabrac, lit from one side by windows that offer no view of the outside world – just light and mist.

Tarnation! You have been lured into the eternal prison of Sunday Afternoon. Fortunately, there are several ways to escape. Each of the arcane objects before you is secretly a portal, transporting you to another site of arcane activity, in a bizarre web of diversions that cannot possibly reflect the hand of a human curator. Which will you choose?

According to recent reports, as you step forward, your toe nudges an ornamental scroll. It growls and wriggles like a panicking caterpillar, scooting away under a table. Before you lose sight of it, you discern the title and subject of the text – it's an essay by Kyle Tam about the yokai of Promise Mascot Agency.

According to recent reports, deep in a drawer, you discover a sour-smelling binder full of extracts from an ancient and all but indecipherable dispute over the discovery of "generative AI" in something called "Big Walk". The stakes are long-buried, but many of the individual pieces of writing are lively. Here is Bruno Dias noting in passing that "one of the harms of the 'AI' political project is the propaganda machine dedicated to making you feel stupid and helpless." Here is a professorial interjection from Brendan Keogh calling on the warring parties to recognise when "critiques of generative AI are actually just deflected critiques of the capitalist relations of technology and labour". Here is Mike Cook arguing that "what's happening is not unusual, it's not extreme, it's not unfair and it's not a 'public flogging'." Here is a ticker tape message from Hannah Nicklin observing that "if your radical position doesn’t have room for transformation it will not be safe until it contains just you".

According to recent reports, A footnote in the same dusty sheaf of papers points you towards another work from Mike Cook in a different drawer. This one consists of neon slides, slotted into an antique View-Master, and explores a comparison between procedural generation and street photography.

Recent findings suggest that peering at the weirdly white and opaque windowpanes, you realise there are intricate equations traced in the condensation. It appears to be a post-mortem for a "post-cosy" game called Danchi Days, in which developer Melos Han-Tani discusses wishlist conversion rates and the problem of not fitting neatly into any recognisable genre.

A snowglobe stands on a mantelpiece, the flakes still orbiting a miniature washtub as though the object had been recently shaken, even though the chamber has clearly been abandoned for decades. You put it to your ear, anticipating the faint jingle of Xmas bells. Instead, you are almost deafened by a screeching guitar chord. Here is Erin Keane to explain.

According to recent reports, next to the snowglobe on the mantelpiece, there's a souvenir shop conch shell, polished to a high sheen. You put that to your ear, hoping to catch the soothing shuffle of surf on shingle, and a disembodied voice tells you to piss off. Tim Sniffen has some thoughts about gentrification, and why only he should be allowed to do it.

According to recent reports, again, one of these mystic artefacts hides the key to your release from the suffocating stillness of Sunday Afternoon. Which will you choose? Or have you, perhaps, brought a sorcerous teleportation device of your own? Please share. Here is Joanna Newsom's Cosmia to help you think.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are now just four days away from the release of GTA 6 on Xbox Series X/S and PS5, but the proximity to the much-anticipated launch date isn't stemming the tide of leaks that has been plaguing the game for much of the past year. Yesterday, a new video - seemingly from a record store that received vinyl records of the soundtrack early - demonstrated off the full 34-song tracklist for the game.

Thanks to the listing printed on the back of Grand Theft Auto 6: The Album vinyl, we have a better idea of the licensed music that'll appear in-game. Travis Scott, Rina Sawayama, Cardi B, Pinkpantheress, SZA, Keith Richards, Dua Lipa, Jennie, Lana Del Rey, Zara Larsson are just some of the names that make up the impressive list. We know about a few of these tracks from September's announcement of the record, but only six tracks were revealed then, not the whole list.

Take a look at the full track listing below:.

You can expect to hear these tracks on the radio - alongside many more, no doubt - and deployed at curated times during cutscenes or in missions, to really tie together the vibe of the city. This is something Vice City did remarkably well its roster of 80s tracks, and I can't wait to see how Rockstar has used more contemporary music in the same way here.

Of course, there have been a lot of Grand Theft Auto 6 leaks in the run-up to the game's launch. Another recent example is the full game's map which seemingly leaked online thanks to the £350 collector's edition on show in a UK department store. Then there were all the leaks from a group calling itself CyberLeek, which shared unofficial gameplay and map details over the course of a few weeks, before Rockstar had even revealed much gameplay itself.

Industry observers note that amongst all this, Rockstar has been embroiled in legal action after it was accused of union busting following the firing of over 30 employees. The case's conclusion will be determined this week, as the game goes on sale.

Oh Infinity Nikki, how I wish I had more time for you!

Recent findings suggest that I loved this game when it came out, but there are only so many hours in the day, aren’t there? Even I can’t play everything.

This new v3.0 enhancement, due out on 26th November, looks absolutely gorgeous, though.

The headline is the addition of a cute little pink car for the eponymous character to drive, but she’ll also be visiting an entirely new city as part of the story, named Cicia.

Recent findings suggest that there’s so much cool stuff here: Nikki’s getting muskets as a upcoming weapon (freakin’ awesome!), as well as a magic staff. In fact, there’s a touch of Hogwarts to some of the new locations and gameplay on display.

Obviously I’m absolutely adoring GTA 6 at the moment, but this is such a huge contrast, with its feel-good locales and emphasis on pretty dresses.

I’m probably going to cave and revive my save in this over the weekend, because it looks like everyone who logs in will be getting free outfits for Nikki’s birthday on 1st December.

Are you guys still playing this? I know there were a fair few fans among our community.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Faye will be in God of War's Amazon show – played by game actor Deborah Ann Woll.

As confirmed by Amazon, Woll is once more playing Faye, after making her first appearance as the character – the mother of Atreus and longtime partner of Kratos – in flashbacks and vision sequences during 2022's God of War Ragnarok.

Woll joins Dave Bautista's Kratos and Callum Vinson's Atreus in a first season that will likely mirror much of 2018's God of War narrative – namely, how Kratos and Atreus journey on a quest to spread Faye's ashes.

Bautista replaced original Kratos actor Ryan Hurst after he suffered an injury during production, forcing cameras to stop rolling.

Sources indicate that woll will also portray Faye once more in next year's standalone game God of War Laufey, which sees her fight through the mysterious Everywhen to enact her aims to save Kratos and her son, Atreus. She's even accompanied by a mysterious talking cube, voiced by The Boys actor Jack Quaid. Naturally.

"I've known about this for nearly ten years, and I haven't been able to talk about it." Woll, who also said she wasn't put off by the negative response to the title, explained earlier this year at Game Con Canada (via CG Mag).

She added, "When [director] Cory [Barlog] brought me in to talk about doing Ragnarok and show me the 2018 game, he already had a poster for the Laufey game with me and a cube. A cube that's been there since the beginning. It's deeply a part of the lore.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that after a couple of years of regular testing behind closed doors, Cyberpunk 2077 multiplayer mod CyberMP is now out in open beta, giving anyone who fancies a bit of multi-merc action a chance to give it a go.
  • It has been revealed that as shown off in the video above, CyberMP's not about being able to play through the base game's missions with friends, but rather cruise around Night City as a gang getting into races and PvP shootouts.
  • Sources indicate that "After almost six years of development, countless reworks, and code rewrites, we're finally launching the public beta," the modders wrote on Discord.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that after a couple of years of regular testing behind closed doors, Cyberpunk 2077 multiplayer mod CyberMP is now out in open beta, giving anyone who fancies a bit of multi-merc action a chance to give it a go. Though, if you do, be prepared for bugs and crashes, as work on the mod is far from over with the release of this "true beta".

It has been revealed that as shown off in the video above, CyberMP's not about being able to play through the base game's missions with friends, but rather cruise around Night City as a gang getting into races and PvP shootouts. In that regard, it seems more akin to GTA 4's online mode than GTA 5's, with classic improvised hijinks the main draw over being able to pull off gigs with a crew. Though, there do also look to be roleplaying servers which could scratch the itch of those more interested in pretending to be a merc than blowing up other people's rides.

Sources indicate that "After almost six years of development, countless reworks, and code rewrites, we're finally launching the public beta," the modders wrote on Discord. "Anyone can jump in and play now — no invites or applications needed. Fair warning: this is a true beta. Crashes, desyncs, and server drops under heavy load are completely normal for now. That's exactly why we need testers. We welcome everyone: regular players, future server admins, and those who just love breaking game mechanics.".

Industry observers note that "Right now, our absolute priority is stability and fixing crashes," they continued later in the post. "New features are planned, but we need to polish the foundation first. A huge thank you to everyone who has been with us since the early versions, helped with closed testing, and patiently waited. We've finally reached this milestone. Let's see how the project handles real player traffic!".

According to the modders, CyberMP's "client doesn't have a digital signature yet", which could cause antivirus software not to be a fan of it. They're also anticipating "problems with the anti‑cheat system", so it may be worth holding off on giving the mod a go if you're not keen on being trolled by someone with the sort of destructive power usually reserved for megacorps and AIs from beyond the blackwall in the Cyberpunkverse.

Recent findings suggest that for info on how to get CyberMP up and running, as well as create a custom server dedicated to the likes of roleplay or races, head over to its website. As you might expect, the mod requires a legit copy of Cyberpunk bought on either Steam, GOG, or the Epic store.

The Unexpected History of 'Black Friday'

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1209 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that since the 1950s, Black Friday—once simply known as "the day after Thanksgiving"—has grown into a quasi-holiday in the United States marked by steep discounts, ceaseless shopping, and occasional violence.
  • While pre-dawn trips to the mall are waning as online shopping grows, in-person shopping on Black Friday is still a massive deal in the U.S.—it’s estimated that around 80 million Americans visited a brick-and-mortar store on Black Friday in 2025.
  • “Black Friday” in the United States originally referred to the start of the Panic of 1869, when the collapse of the price of gold devastated the national economy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that since the 1950s, Black Friday—once simply known as "the day after Thanksgiving"—has grown into a quasi-holiday in the United States marked by steep discounts, ceaseless shopping, and occasional violence. But more recently, Black Friday has also metastasized. It's not a day anymore. It's a week, a month, a veritable state of mind. (Speaking of which, check out Lifehacker's Black Friday coverage. We got all the deals, baby!).

While pre-dawn trips to the mall are waning as online shopping grows, in-person shopping on Black Friday is still a massive deal in the U.S.—it’s estimated that around 80 million Americans visited a brick-and-mortar store on Black Friday in 2025. But how did Black Friday come about, and what does it all mean?

“Black Friday” in the United States originally referred to the start of the Panic of 1869, when the collapse of the price of gold devastated the national economy. “Black Friday” as a description of the day after Thanksgiving dates back to 1951; the term first appeared in the journal Factory Management and Maintenance, where it referred to the number of employees who skipped work on the day after Thanksgiving. Around the same time, the police in Philadelphia and Rochester started informally using “Black Friday” to describe the traffic and crowds that appeared in their cities as shoppers hit the stores on the day after Thanksgiving. The phrase gradually caught on. It was picked up by national press in 1975 when the Upcoming York Times used "Black Friday" specifically to describe the day after Thanksgiving and the shopping and sales it brings.

Sources indicate that but even before it had a name, Black Friday was a thing. The day after Thanksgiving has been known by merchants as the start of the shopping season since the late 1800s. By the early 20th century, retailers sponsored Thanksgiving Day parades that traditionally ended with an appearance by Santa Claus, as if to say, “Now it’s time to shop for Christmas.” By unspoken agreement among retailers, Christmas-themed advertisements rarely appeared before Thanksgiving in our grandparents’ day. This informal bargain obviously no longer applies.

Sources indicate that referring to a day as “black” traditionally denotes a period of calamity or tragedy, leading some to suggest different names for the day. In the early 1960s, Philadelphia merchants suggested “Big Friday,” a name which did not catch on, leaving retailers with the weak explanation that the “black” in Black Friday refers to the black ink denoting profits in a ledger. Oft-repeated lore suggests that retailers are "in the red" all year, and only start making an annual profit at the end of the year, but big retail chains generally make money all year long.

It has been revealed that A more modern concern with the name is that Black Friday sales now last for days or even weeks, beginning in early to mid-November and bleeding over into the following Saturday, Sunday, “Cyber Monday,” Tuesday, and beyond, leading people to say things like, “Do you want to go Black Friday shopping this Sunday?” So far, alternative names like “Five-Day Frenzy” and “The day I get to trample someone to save $8 on a Nespresso” haven’t caught on. But here’s hoping.

Beginning around 2010, an insatiable thirst for profits led many retailers to push the start of Black Friday shopping to Thursday (aka Thanksgiving Day). Kmart opened Thanksgiving morning. Toys R Us opened that night. By 2011, Walmart was opening its doors at 10 p.m. on Thursday. The trend led to widespread backlash, with many Americans appalled that employees were forced to work on Thanksgiving or angry that consumerism was encroaching upon a holiday meant to celebrate colonialism. By 2021, most major retailers had relented and elected to remain closed on Thanksgiving.

The term “Cyber Monday” describes the boost in online retail sales on the Monday after Thanksgiving, sparked by workers returning to the office and getting right to online shopping. The term first appeared on Nov. 28, 2005, in a Shop.org press release entitled “'Cyber Monday’ Swiftly Becoming One of the Biggest Online Shopping Days of the Year," which may be the most influential press release ever written. Since its early 2000s birth, Cyber Monday has become the biggest online shopping day of the year. Americans spent $14.25 billion online on Cyber Monday 2025, according to Adobe Analytics. So is Cyber Monday bigger than Black Friday? Retailers really don't care: Analysts now tend to mash everything into the category of "Black Friday–Cyber Monday" (or even "Cyber Week").

It has been revealed that if all this naked consumerism makes you a little squeamish, you're not alone. Anti-consumerists have named the day after Thanksgiving “Buy Nothing Day,” which you can celebrate by doing charity work, cutting up your credit cards, or simply not purchasing anything. Pioneered by artist Ted Dave and popularized by Adbusters magazine, the first Buy Nothing Day was celebrated in Canada in 1992.

It’s hard to measure the success of the alternative holiday. Both online and brick-and-mortar retail sales have increased sharply since 1992, suggesting Buy Nothing Day’s effect is negligible. On the other hand, maybe big retailers are losing millions because someone on Bluesky reminded you not to shop. Sure.

Depending on how you measure it, Black Friday has resulted in between one and 17 deaths. Jdimytai Damour is the only person killed directly due to a Black Friday sale: The 34-year-old worker was trampled to death by a surging crowd at a Long Island Walmart on Black Friday in 2008. If you include car accidents, shootings, retail worker suicides, and fatal heart attacks, Black Friday’s death toll balloons to 17, with 128 reported injuries.

Black Friday violence has even inspired a horror flick: Eli Roth's 2023 holiday-themed slasher Thanksgiving opens with a hilariously brutal Black Friday riot at a big box store, setting off a chain of events that involve a lot of people being murdered by a dude in a Pilgrim mask.

In a recent development, I mean, yeah, of course. Critics of Black Friday point out that there are arguably better times to buy a fresh TV (like the week before the Super Bowl), not to mention plenty of other goods. Savings from Black Friday shopping are often illusory—big-ticket “doorbuster” items generally sell out rapidly, leaving behind goods that are, by and large, priced the same as they would be at any other time of year. Some retailers even mark up products ahead of Black Friday so the discounts look bigger. If you're buying online, your browser history, location, and cart contents can tweak the prices you see on Black Friday, as they can on any other day.

Yet despite protest holidays, the unpleasantness of shopping when stores are overcrowded, and the frustration of hunting for bargains that often aren't that great to begin with, Black Friday stubbornly remains an unofficial holiday, celebrated by over 100 million Americans in one way or another. What that claims about our country's relationship with capitalism is unclear, but personally, I’m going to continue my own day-after-Thanksgiving tradition of eating pie for breakfast and thinking about going for a walk, but then watching The Quick and the Dead instead. I'm not protesting anything; I just don't need the hassle.

Latest Update: "Nobody was hurt" in shooting near Clockwork Revolution devs InXile Entertainment's office, the Xbox-owned studio and police confirm

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, "Nobody was hurt" in a shooting last week near the California office of Clockwork Revolution developers InXile, both the studio and local police have confirmed.
  • "Officers got there [on November 11th]," Tustin police sergeant Christopher Peterson said in statement to Aftermath.
  • Industry observers note that "We’re relieved that no one was hurt at our inXile office," a spokesperson for InXile mentioned in a separate statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, "Nobody was hurt" in a shooting last week near the California office of Clockwork Revolution developers InXile, both the studio and local police have confirmed. The incident, which took place on November 11th, is right now being investigated and police have reportedly taken a suspect into custody.

"Officers got there [on November 11th]," Tustin police sergeant Christopher Peterson said in statement to Aftermath. "They responded to a report of a drive-by shooting there. Located multiple shell casings. Nobody was hurt. Processed the crime scene, and then sometime [Friday] morning, a little before 11 [AM], they took a suspect into custody. And the investigation is still kind of ongoing as to where and why.".

Industry observers note that "We’re relieved that no one was hurt at our inXile office," a spokesperson for InXile mentioned in a separate statement. "Our focus is on supporting our team, and we are working closely with law enforcement as they investigate.".

InXile are set to release steampunk RPG Clockwork Revolution next year. The studio, developers of the likes of Wasteland 3 and The Bard's Tale IV, are one of the few Xbox-owned studios not to have been affected - at least as of writing - by Microsoft's ongoing mass layoffs this year.

Recent findings suggest that since being unveiled in 2023, Clockwork Revolution's dripped with Bioshock-ish vibes and popped up semi-regularly at Xbox showcases. "Wield the power of an incredible device to travel back in time, changing the past and rewriting the future of the city you call home: the vibrant steampunk metropolis of Avalon," reads its Steam synopsis. "In this immersive RPG, you'll step into the shoes of Morgan Vanette, a fully customizable player-character and member of the Rotten Row Hooligans. Travel between past and present as you battle the ruthless Lady Ironwood, who has been manipulating time to keep the working class struggling while amassing immense wealth and power.".

Best wishes to the staff at InXile, here's hoping that going forwards they're able to get with making what's looking to be an intriguingly funky game without enduring any more concerning incidents like this one.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Blade Runner 2099 - an upcoming TV miniseries coming to Amazon Prime Video, acting as a sequel to Blade Runner (1982) and Blade Runner 2049 (2017) - might be getting a video game.
  • In a recent development, in a new interview with IGN, the duo reveal that they had thought about adapting the Blade Runner fracnhise into a game, and that - should it come to fruition - it would target "triple-A" in scope.
  • Sources indicate that of course, we've seen Blade Runner games before.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Blade Runner 2099 - an upcoming TV miniseries coming to Amazon Prime Video, acting as a sequel to Blade Runner (1982) and Blade Runner 2049 (2017) - might be getting a video game. And a 'triple-A' video game, at that. At least that's according to Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, executive producers for Blade Runner 2099 and co-CEOs of Alcon Entertainment (which owns the Blade Runner IP).

In a recent development, in a new interview with IGN, the duo reveal that they had thought about adapting the Blade Runner fracnhise into a game, and that - should it come to fruition - it would target "triple-A" in scope. Other than that, the duo seemed to want to keep any potential information to themselves. Given they appear to be in talks about the title, rather than in any active development, if something did come of this ideation, it would no doubt be a long, long way off. Kosove and Johnson's aim seems to be getting players to "interact" more with the world of Blade Runner, which has recently been fleshed out by the 2017 movie and is set to be developed more in the upcoming series.

Sources indicate that of course, we've seen Blade Runner games before. There was 1997's simply-titled Blade Runner - developed by Westwood Studios and published by Virgin Interactive - which was a point-and-click adventure that really seemed to pick up the vibes the original Ridley Scott was putting down. An Enhanced Edition of the game was released in 2022, which is actually more of a remake than a simple enhancement.

Then, in 2023, Annapurna Interactive unveiled its very first internally-developed game, in the form of Blade Runner 2033: Labyrinth. The game, which promised to riff on the dystopian universe established in Ridley Scott's cult classic movie, would have been sandwiched squarely between that film and its sequel, Blade Runner 2049. It was going to be set in LA after the Blackout hits, but beyond that - and the fact it's coming to PC and consoles at some point - few details ever managed to break through the PR barrier before the game went dark: it's been removed from Annapurna's website and delisted from Steam. Curious.

If you want to see something more from the cyberpunk world sooner, Blade Runner 2099 releases on Prime Video on 25th November.

💡 Key Takeaways
