  • “With Wuling’s story wrapping up, and the main story taking us through all the heavy moments, we want to give you a change of pace with a lighthearted, upbeat patch,” stated Arknights: Endfield producer Light Zhong in a press release.
  • Version Update “Meeting You in the World o’Shrooms”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that publisher GRYPHLINE and developer Mountain Contour will release the version enhancement “Meeting You in the World o’Shrooms” for free-to-play 3D RPG Arknights: Endfield on November 25, the companies announced. The game’s latest live stream also introduced the upcoming version 2.0 update, which takes players to Gypsosia and aboard the Rhodes Island landship, and teased 10 characters who will join the journey across upcoming content updates.

“With Wuling’s story wrapping up, and the main story taking us through all the heavy moments, we want to give you a change of pace with a lighthearted, upbeat patch,” stated Arknights: Endfield producer Light Zhong in a press release.

Here is an overview of the update, via GRYPHLINE:.

Version Update “Meeting You in the World o’Shrooms”.

Strange mushrooms have overrun an abandoned dam outside Wuling, where Landbreakers worship a giant mushroom and visitors keep slipping into hallucinations. There, the Endministrator meets Kay, a Rhodes Island Operator who has been adventuring alone across Talos-II in search of them. Kay happily shares everything she treasures, including a towering stack of honey waffles. But which would she choose: a mountain of waffles or a dear friend?

A Nature Vanguard with a carefree fighting style, Kay throws weapons that scatter across the battlefield, then gathers them up for a heavy hammer slam. Along the way, she drops Picnic Snacks that heal her teammates.

The Old Dam, the enhancement’s new area, has grown into a fairytale-like mushroom kingdom. Players fire Kay’s honey waffles at mushrooms to open doors and spin fungal bridges, and must avoid Loquacious Shrooms that scramble their sense of direction. Mushroom foes like the Bolete Prince guard the dam, and a mushroom as tall as a mountain waits at its heart.

The enhancement’s music leans into its whimsical tone, with Ori composer Gareth Coker and ambient producer Owsey returning to score Kay’s honey waffle adventure. It caps a first year in which the soundtrack has followed the story, from the sweeping sci-fi orchestral sound of Valley IV to the choir-driven battle against Alleikhreos, Typhoeus’s JRPG-inspired winter journey and the modern electronic take on Eastern music in Si’s painted world.

According to recent reports, later in the revision, every player who logs in during the Workers’ Guards: Roll Call event will receive the Operator Mimino and her signature weapon, Star of Tomorrow, for free, with event missions offering extra copies to reach full Potential. Operators Gilberta and Rossi also return in successive reruns.

For factory builders, Exclusion Zone Rebuilding is a newly introduced permanent mode in which players supply materials across four phases to restore the North Wuling Exclusion Zone, using the new Forge of Luminance to transform products on their conveyor belts. For a lighter break, Lucky Carrot’s Games of Wonder adds two multiplayer card games, Witch’s Darkjack and Band Uprising, that players can enjoy with friends or through matchmaking.

A First Look at Version 2.0 and Rhodes Island.

The livestream also previewed the next chapter of Arknights: Endfield, arriving in the new year. Exiles have introduced attacks across the Civilization Band, and their real target is Rhodes Island. The Endministrator sets out with Perlica into Gypsosia, the Cretaceous Frontiers, where players will be able to board and explore Rhodes Island itself, a massive landship. A 10-character teaser offered a glimpse of companions for the journey, including Warfarin, appearing as the leader of Rhodes Island, and M3, who returns looking completely different.

According to recent reports, the chapter’s first update will add four newly introduced maps at once, including Rhodes Island. Main Mission Early Unlock: Gypsosia will let players who have completed the main mission Remediation Progress skip ahead to the new story while still earning all beginner-event rewards. New modes are also in development for future updates, including a management sim with the Golden Branch Tribe and the Shattered Protocol combat mode.

According to recent reports, arknights: Endfield is now Steam Deck Verified, with default controller support and every feature available on Valve’s handheld. The revision also brings Despot Weaponized, a newly introduced high-difficulty challenge series in Umbral Monument; the return of RISE! MEGA ARENA!, a two-Operator arena event; and new seasons of the Echoes of War combat mode.

Arknights: Endfield is available now for PlayStation 5, PC via the official launcher, Steam, and Epic Games Store, iOS via App Store, and Android via Google Play.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Use of generative AI in game dev remains as contentious as it does ubiquitous—a recent GDC report found that around 40% of devs use AI, but more than half think its influence has been negative. Ubisoft is continuing to double down on the technology, this time with Motherbrain, a fresh subsidiary fashioned from the team behind its "first playable generative AI experience.".

As reported by VGC, Motherbrain's purpose is to develop "AI for gameplay innovation, supporting all game creators in developing groundbreaking experiences … Its current focus is on upcoming player experiences, smart NPCs with memory and AI game masters that manage large scale systemic worlds," according to an earnings report which was released Thursday.

The information comes at a turbulent time for the publishing giant, which just laid off 166 employees even after Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced "outperformed expectations." A sweeping internal overhaul earlier this year saw the company reorganize its workforce into a throng of "creative houses," a decision which led to swathes of layoffs and six project cancellations, including the Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time Remake.

Industry observers note that it's not clear what Motherbrain are at work on, in specific terms, right now, but there may be some clues in its past work. That playable AI "experience" I mentioned earlier is none other than Teammates, an R&D project based on a prior experiment with uncanny AI "neo-NPCs.".

Industry observers note that teammates aimed to allow players to command NPC squadmates in a rudimentary shooter game with a microphone, and using AI, have those squadmates react believably. It's not far off, at least conceptually, from what we've seen in games like Where Winds Meet and Fortnite, both of which have experimented with AI-powered NPCs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Xbox Project Helix, the next (mysterious) console underway from Microsoft, has been in the limelight recently for its support of PC games – support that was reportedly far more fleshed out during the hardware's initial conception.

Jason Ronald, vice president of Xbox's gaming devices and ecosystem team, recently noted that Project Helix is "a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC," as "it's really designed to be the ultimate gaming machine." That sounds pretty dang capable already, but apparently, it was supposed to feature even more PC integration – think full-on free online multiplayer access, Steam, and the like.

Anonymous sources tell Windows Central as much, alleging that the original initiative – one operating underneath a different codename – for the console was for it to essentially be a gaming computer that can also run Xbox games… on top of PC titles on storefronts like Valve's own Steam. Think the ASUS ROG Xbox Ally, for example, albeit not handheld. I'm reminded of the Steam Machine, personally, although that notably doesn't run on Windows.

The supposed predecessor to Project Helix would work with a gamepad-centered Xbox-style full-screen interface (like Steam's Big Picture Mode, for example), allowing users to exit out to a normal Windows desktop and run other programs such as Steam.

Furthermore, the report states the console would've been free to play online – no extra subscriptions or fees like Sony's PlayStation Plus service required to engage in multiplayer games.

That would mean no Xbox Game Pass paywall, as a PC wouldn't… well, work with a paywall at all, really. This wouldn't have been a cheap decision for Microsoft, and that paired with a move toward another hardware strategy, changes in management, and more, likely contributed to a reshuffle of prepares – if this intriguing computer-esque console ever truly was on the table, that is. It does all beg the question: what will Project Helix look like?

I suppose we won't know until it's finally here. Let's just hope it doesn't cost as much as $1,800 – one rumored price point I can't quite get out of my head. For now, I think I'll just stick to my good ol' actual PC.

Xbox Project Helix lead says it's "one of the most exciting times" to be making a new console, because the "challenging" component crisis means finding new ways to balance innovation and accessibility.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Treyarch's former Senior lead writer, Craig Houston, has been laid off after approximately 20 years of service with the developer.
  • "After approximately 20 years, I was sadly one of those affected by recent layoffs," he noted in his posts.
  • Sources indicate that on Twitter/X, he quote tweeted a video celebrating 30 years of Treyarch and featuring footage from many of the games he worked on to share his message.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Treyarch's former Senior lead writer, Craig Houston, has been laid off after approximately 20 years of service with the developer. In a post made to both his Twitter/X account and LinkedIn, the developer thanked fans for their support during his two decades with the company and confirmed he was impacted by recent reorganistation within the studio.

"After approximately 20 years, I was sadly one of those affected by recent layoffs," he noted in his posts. "I am proud to have worked with so many talented people - many of whom will remain friends for life. Thanks to all the fans for your enthusiasm, support, and kind words over the years.".

Sources indicate that on Twitter/X, he quote tweeted a video celebrating 30 years of Treyarch and featuring footage from many of the games he worked on to share his message. It appears the layoffs referenced are part of the broad reorganistation affecting 3200 jobs that Xbox declared earlier this year. Treyarch, as part of Activision Blizzard, is owned by Xbox.

Houston is a bonafide veteran of the esteemed FPS series. His first Call of Duty title at Treyarch was Call of Duty 3, where he worked as a video editor. This was followed by World at War, Black Ops 1 through 4, where he is credited as a writer and designer. For Modern Warfare, Black Ops - Cold War, Vanguard, Modern Warfare 3, then Black Ops 6 and 7, he is listed as a member of the design team and in 'creative development'. He is not credited on this year's Modern Warfare 4.

Industry observers note that if you've picked up a Call of Duty game in the past decade-plus, you'll have interacted with Houston's work: he was a central creative force behind the writing for Treyarch's campaign modes since 2006 (with Call of Duty 3) and the main writer for the Zombies mode since 2008 (with Call of Duty: World at War). Alongside Jimmy Zielinski, Jason Blundell, and Kevin Drew, Houston was an integral part of the evolution of the Zombies pillar of Call of Duty, and shaped it into the series-defining thing it is today. There has been a fair amount of community support for Houston since he announced the news yesterday; he was a popular dev, and a lot of the Zombies-specific fan communities online hold a lot of respect for him.

"Craig is a great guy," notes one user on Reddit. "You can tell how much he loves the story/characters he writes just by how excited he is when he talks about them in promo material.".

Industry observers note that "You're a Legend Craig, it was an honor to work with you," says ex-Treyarch vet, Tony Flame, in a reply to Houston's X post. "You created a truly special experience that will live on in the kinds of millions fans. Wishing you the best [...].".

From all of us here at Eurogamer, and myself personally - who really admires the character-work and emergent storytelling present in the Xbox 360-era Call of Duty games, specifically - we wish you the best and good luck with the future, Craig.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh Cyberpunk 2077 mod has overhauled Night City's rain, swapping the game's flat wet weather effects for individual 3D drops and adding lightning storms.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh Cyberpunk 2077 mod has overhauled Night City's rain, swapping the game's flat wet weather effects for individual 3D drops and adding lightning storms.

Sources indicate that as spotted by DSOGaming, modder CyanideX's mod, Torrent, gives each raindrop its own size and falling speed. The drops also react to the player's movement, so they stream towards the windscreen when you're driving fast. If you find the wind has picked up, blustery weather can also push them sideways, too.

The rain also catches the light from street lamps, neon signs, car headlights, and taillights, and won't fall through roofs or inside buildings. Drops splash on the ground, heavy rain leaves mist in the distance, and cars throw up spray from their tyres on wet roads.

The mod complements this with a new lightning system, with branching bolts that flash and flicker before fading, and that can arrive in bursts during heavier storms.

If you like a little lightning, the frequency of bolts can be adjusted across 10 levels, and with the AudioXL mod installed, thunder follows each strike, timed to how far away it landed.

For players sensitive to flashing lights, a Reduce Flashes option dims the lightning, replaces its flicker with a single slow glow, and halves the number of strikes.

Recent findings suggest that torrent supports Nova City 2 and other weather mods, and adds extra storm effects for Nova City 2 players, including mist that rolls through the streets with the wind. It’s available now on Nexus Mods.

  • The BBC report that, on November 16th, Arion Kurtaj pleaded guilty at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar Games hack and a number of others he carried out with the hacking gang Lapsus$ while aged 16 and 17.
  • Sources indicate that kurtaj carried out the 2022 Rockstar hack while on bail for other hacking offences and being housed at a Travelodge hotel under police protection, the latter on account of rival hackers threatening to attack him over stolen Bitcoin stashes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A hacker has pleaded guilty to a number of online crimes, including the 2022 breach of Rockstar Games which resulted in a bunch of mid-development clips of GTA 6 in action leaking onto the net.

The BBC report that, on November 16th, Arion Kurtaj pleaded guilty at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar Games hack and a number of others he carried out with the hacking gang Lapsus$ while aged 16 and 17. Kurtaj, now aged 21, was previously sentenced to stay in a secure hospital indefinitely due to the severity of his autism, but was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial. He'll be sentenced at a later date.

Sources indicate that kurtaj carried out the 2022 Rockstar hack while on bail for other hacking offences and being housed at a Travelodge hotel under police protection, the latter on account of rival hackers threatening to attack him over stolen Bitcoin stashes. The Rockstar hack was reportedly done using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into the hotel room's TV, plus a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse.

90 clips of unfinished GTA 6 were flung online by that hack, with Rockstar having refused to cooperate with Kurtaj's demand via an internal Slack channel that the company contact him on massaging app Telegram within 24 hours. Rockstar claimed the breach cost them $5m million to recover from, in addition to staff having to waste thousands of hours.

Industry observers note that earlier this year, GTA 6 suffered yet another leak, with a hacker or hackers going by "Cyberleek" posting various videos of the game in action. Rockstar and parent organization Take-Two promptly sprung into action, taking down videos, filing subpoenas, and issuing a statement that called the leak "heartbreaking".

Hopefully with the game's console release later this week, those will be the only two GTA 6 leaks which have to be added to the annals of gaming history. As much as marketing can leave a bad taste in the mouth, especially when it barely indicates anything of the actual product being advertised, neither of the GTA 6 leaks served much of a purpose beyond forcing people to waste some time and energy talking about the perpetrators.

According to Aftermath, officers responded to reports of a drive-by shooting at Flight at Tustin Legacy, a campus that houses inXile and other businesses, on 11th November.

InXile is the studio behind the Wasteland series, and is currently working on Clockwork Revolution.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • EA has made some notable leadership changes within its studios group, and in who oversees the Battlefield franchise.
  • Beede confirmed the change on LinkedIn, saying that he now oversees EA's shooter and action-RPG portfolio, seemingly occupying the role of the late Vince Zampella.
  • In this stead, EA appointed Sam Cooper as Battlefield's new boss.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

EA has made some notable leadership changes within its studios group, and in who oversees the Battlefield franchise. Byron Beede, previously Battlefield's general manager, has been promoted to group general manager.

Beede confirmed the change on LinkedIn, saying that he now oversees EA's shooter and action-RPG portfolio, seemingly occupying the role of the late Vince Zampella.

In this stead, EA appointed Sam Cooper as Battlefield's new boss. Cooper, who also revealed his new job title on LinkedIn, previously had a stint at EA Sports, but he's mostly known for his work at Activision, where he spent the last five-ish years as Call of Duty's global product management and head of live service.

While this might seem like fairly unremarkable corporate news - executives move between rival companies all the time, after all - it reinforces a narrative that EA continues to keenly replicate Activision's Call of Duty model.

It has been revealed that that particular push is years-old now, and it kicked off in 2021 when EA hired Byron Beede, former boss of all of Call of Duty at Activision, to lead the next evolution of Battlefield. So far, that decision has given us the very successful Battlefield 6 and its free-to-play, COD: Warzone-like battle royale mode Redsec.

Sources indicate that to facilitate that, EA rearranged several of its studios to serve under one banner dubbed Battlefield Studios, replicating Activision's model of locking several teams around the world into developing and supporting a single game / franchise. Ripple Effect, Motive, the iconic Criterion and, of course, series creator DICE are all the Battlefield franchise's lead and support studios.

Many players argue - and I would agree - that Battlefield and Call of Duty games are more alike today than they've ever been. The user interface, the emphasis on limited-time events, the garish store cosmetics, the COD-like battle pass system - complete with a more expensive option, are all signs of that transition. And that is to say nothing of controversial changes to longstanding Battlefield tenets, such as the class system, intended to make Battlefield 6 appeal to a wider audience.

The effects of that leadership change likely won't materialise until the next Battlefield title, but it's a curious one to keep in mind as EA leans even harder into its biggest franchises following its $55bn private equity and Saudi Arabia's PIF-funded buyout.

Intel are being sued for "misleading" investors about "a massive glut of unwanted PC inventory" thanks to AI-fuelled price hikes

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that tech giant Intel are being taken to court for allegedly "misleading" their investors about the sheer scale of the impact of generative AI-fuelled component price hikes on PC sales.
  • All this follows Intel's last round of quarterly results, in which they confirmed a significant revenue fall; this triggered an Intel stock price drop from $92.07 per share on October 29th to $65.76 per share the next day, which this week's lawsuit characterises as "the largest single-day price decline for Intel common stock in over 50 years".
  • The lawyers in question are from Robbins LLP, who specialise in "shareholder, whistleblower, antitrust, & consumer litigation".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that tech giant Intel are being taken to court for allegedly "misleading" their investors about the sheer scale of the impact of generative AI-fuelled component price hikes on PC sales. The class action lawsuit in question claims that Intel's distribution and manufacturing partners have had to deal with "a massive glut of unwanted PC inventory", and that the gains from Intel's investments in AI datacenters aren't enough to make up for slowing sales of PCs to regular Josephines who just want fancy boxes they can play Deadlock on.

All this follows Intel's last round of quarterly results, in which they confirmed a significant revenue fall; this triggered an Intel stock price drop from $92.07 per share on October 29th to $65.76 per share the next day, which this week's lawsuit characterises as "the largest single-day price decline for Intel common stock in over 50 years".

The lawyers in question are from Robbins LLP, who specialise in "shareholder, whistleblower, antitrust, & consumer litigation". In a press release, they say they've filed suit on behalf of anybody who bought Intel stock from July 23rd to October 29th this year.

The suit claims that Intel neglected to tell investors that falling PC and component sales were having a "materially greater negative impact" on their third financial quarter 2026 Client Computing and Physical AI Groupresults than Intel had previously stated – to the tune of "hundreds of millions of dollars" in revenue shrinkage, compared to the previous quarter, with the situation still expected to "worsen".

They also accuse the organization of keeping schtum about the aforesaid "massive glut of unwanted PC inventory", together with the fact that "any positive impacts to Intel’s business and financial results resulting from data center construction and other aspects of the AI boom were more than offset by the negative effects on the Company’s business and financial results resulting from the PC market slowdown and the excess inventory buildup described above.".

Finally, they say Intel bosses have failed to disclose that they're struggling to procure an adequate supply of substrates – that is, materials used to create the base layer of chips, circuit boards and similar components. As such, the lawyers claim, Intel couldn't "ramp up production to meet data center CPU demand even if the Company chose to divert production resources because of a slowdown in PC-related sales.".

Sources indicate that once the Godzilla of personal computing, Intel haven't been having a brilliant few years. Back in 2024, they recorded a multi-billion dollar quarterly loss, pushing then-CEO Pat Gelsinger to resign. As regards sales of gaming PCs, they've fallen behind AMD, though they've reportedly taken some ground back recently as regards desktop CPUs. As regards graphics cards, they have long been dwarfed by Nvidia.

Cyberagent - the parent company of Umamusume: Pretty Derby developer Cygames - has boasted its recent successes in the mobile gaming sphere in a recent quarterly earnings presentation.

Recent findings suggest that as part of this presentation (covered by Automaton), the company has established aims to launch seven "major releases" to the mobile platform by 2030. There is no word on what these games will be, but one will be released in 2027, while another two will come in 2028.

Cyberagent boasted an 88 percent "hit" rate for its mobile releases so far, with seven of its eight releases having a development budget of around a billion yen, and reaching a point where it makes that figure back every month from its playerbases. Sources indicate that cyberAgent CEO Takahiro Yamauchi - speaking during the presentation - noted that it was still difficult to predict the success of a mobile game ahead of its release. However, he also claims that the experience Cyberagent has gained with its substantial releases to date have allowed the firm to gain a clearer perspective on profitability and sustainability.

This presentation comes after a notable month for Cygmes and Umamusume: Pretty Derby. The developer issued refunds for hotels and flights following the sudden cancellation of an LA live show for the game last month, then shortly after became a major sponsor of the Japanese Formula 1 Grand Prix. The game was also temporarily taken offline due to the major PHP vulnerability exposed last month, an outage that was thankfully short-lived.

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the ROG Xbox Ally X20 makes for a fantastic upgrade over last year's vanilla X predecessor, but its higher price tag keeps it from getting any closer to portable perfection.
  • Elevated controls that feel like a real Xbox controller.
  • Same great performance from Ryzen Z2 Extreme as before.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the ROG Xbox Ally X20 makes for a fantastic upgrade over last year's vanilla X predecessor, but its higher price tag keeps it from getting any closer to portable perfection. Additions like its vibrant latest OLED 1080P 120Hz display and controls that feel far more like an official console controller help justify its MSRP, but it's still going to be out of reach for plenty of players who deserve a solid portable PC experience.

Fantastically vibrant OLED display.

Elevated controls that feel like a real Xbox controller.

Same great performance from Ryzen Z2 Extreme as before.

Slight enhancements to ergonomics via rubber grips and subtle changes.

Xbox Major Screen Experience helps dilute pain of Windows 11.

$1,300 is arguably too much for any handheld.

No real performance improvements over last year's model.

In a recent development, why you can trust GamesRadar+ Our experts review games, movies and tech over countless hours, so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about our reviews policy.

Sources indicate that some say second time’s the charm; I tend to think third time’s lucky, but the ROG Xbox Ally X20 technically isn’t really a redo of Microsoft’s handheld gaming PC. Yes, it switches out the old 1080p 120Hz IPS display with the OLED panel it should have had in the first place and adds fancy new TMR sticks, but the upgrades feel geared toward a select few who’re actively willing to spend over $1,000 on a portable in 2026.

It has been revealed that that is to say that while adding an OLED display to last year’s ROG Xbox Ally X absolutely elevates the visual experience and thoroughly pleased my peepers during testing, the X20’s price tag holds it back. If money were not an object, I’d automatically give the revamp its predecessor’s seat at the best gaming handheld table, but alas, paying $1,299.99 / £1,399.99 for the newbie comes down to your feelings about enhanced brightness and vibrancy.

Industry observers note that yes, this is the same “sweating button guy” meme situation sparked by the Steam Deck OLED back in 2024, so I’m not saying making a shiny new ROG Xbox X20 was a bad idea. In fact, throughout my time testing this new Ryzen Z2 Extreme contender, I’ve fallen even harder for its chonky controller grips and even its less-than-perfect console-inspired Xbox Big Screen Experience. The main problem is that, unlike when Valve popped a new panel on its portable, Asus and Microsoft have ramped up the price by $300.

In a recent development, I have a terrible relationship with time. I struggle with the passage of time and how quickly a calendar year loops back around. You could even call it a phobia, so upon grabbing onto the ROG Xbox Ally X20 for the first time, I was immediately hit with an eerie wave of Déjà vu that made me realize that the “OG” ROG Xbox Ally X was now 12 months old. However, rather than feeling like I’d blinked through into the future, I instead felt like I was back, taking a look at Microsoft’s portable for the first time.

I’m not for one second saying Asus should have overhauled its design language for the Xbox Ally X20. In fact, I’m thrilled that the handheld is hanging onto all of its evolved ergonomics, like its controller-inspired back grips, asymmetrical thumbstick layout, and visual cues that are closer to the PlayStation Portal than its portable PC kin.

According to recent reports, at the same time, some players will be asking “what’s changed” with the ROG Xbox Ally X20, and while it does sport a rather dashing smoked transparent shell and gold accents, you’d be forgiven for thinking it’s just a newly introduced colorway. It technically is, but when you’re paying $300 more than the last time, and technically more again compared to the OG Asus ROG Ally, most players will want it to scream, “I am worth the hike.”.

Let’s just say that on the aesthetics front, I’m pretty baffled that Microsoft decided not to nostalgia-bait players with a transparent green shell and OG Xbox-inspired face buttons. I’d pretty much assumed something similar to the X25 controller was a given, and I do think that, on its own, doesn’t justify a hike; it would have helped it feel more like a celebratory “special edition” 25th anniversary release. Instead, the “X20” is actually in honor of Asus’ Republic of Gamers brand and its 20th anniversary, which is, uh, perhaps not in your calendar if you’re here for the console vibes.

Recent findings suggest that if we’re talking purple about looks and feel, and you’re deliberating between the ROG Xbox Ally X20 and its vanilla X sibling, here are my observations on the subtleties. In the hands, the X20 manages to feel slightly posher, largely thanks to rubberized back grips and an increase in heft (756g vs 715g). The gold accents only just dodge garish accusations, and while the retro console editor in me naturally digs translucent tech, the smoke show only gives a slight glimpse of its innards under the right lighting conditions.

Sources indicate that with that increased weight, I did find myself balancing my elbows on things more with the X20 compared to the original. It’s not aggressively heavier, and the rubber grips did help provide enhanced stability overall, especially when holding on for my life in Star Wars Galactic Racer. But otherwise, you’re talking about two handhelds that feel nearly identical to clutch, and the reasons to splurge on the newbie aren’t shell-deep.

According to recent reports, I’m not quite done covering how the ROG Xbox Ally X20 feels to use, as Asus and Microsoft have done far more with the buttons, triggers, and sticks than you’d perhaps expect. Effectively, the handheld now feels almost like an actual Xbox controller rather than drawing influence from a third-party pad like the Asus ROG Raikiri Pro. The result is something that absolutely translates to a portable console experience, and it’s perhaps what we should have got the first time around.

In a recent development, I’ll note that the face buttons and sticks are virtually the same as before, but the latter does swap out traditional parts for TMR (Tunnel Magnetoresistance) tech, resulting in an accuracy boost and natural immunity to stick drift. The A,B,X,Y buttons feature the same snappy membranes as before, and since I had zero complaints with them before, it feels right that they made it to this second revision.

The real showstopper lies with the X20’s D-pad, triggers, and bumpers, as those now magically feel just like an Xbox Wireless Controller. The concave D-pad and its clicky dome contacts have finally usurped Asus's old design, meaning you’re getting all the tactile goodness the console provides to side-scroller lovers and fighting game enthusiasts alike. Even if you’re not into genres that explicitly leverage it, the added tactility and accuracy make all the difference when used as a toggle, with, again, Galactic Racer really shining when flicking speeder switches at the start of each race.

Sources indicate that xbox controllers also provide a very distinct set of triggers with dampening qualities, and while it’s included to dial back plasticky clunks, it also contributes to a very specific feel. The Xbox Ally X did attempt to emulate this, and I figured it had gotten pretty close to emulating the results. That was until I started playing on the X20 and swiftly realized there was room for improvement, as my brain instantly registered each trigger press as being just like my Robot White pad.

There’s admittedly not that much in the feel of the X20 controls vs. the X, but there’s enough to matter. Everything from the bounce of those triggers to the newly introduced-age Xbox D-pad helps reinforce the brand’s presence with this portable, and that’s really important when you’re clearly trying to target console players with dreams of playing their libraries on the go.

Industry observers note that look, it shouldn’t really be a surprise that the ROG Xbox Ally X20’s main selling point is the OLED screen, especially given that the accompanying specs haven’t changed. For what it’s worth, the switch-out makes for a tremendous visual experience that is geared to take on the Steam Deck OLED and win thanks to its 1080p 120Hz capabilities and higher brightness.

There are objective metrics that help spell out the OLED benefits on paper, like the fact you’re getting a larger 1080p 120Hz 7.4-inch panel that provides 297 pixels per inch with 1,400 nits HDR brightness (600 nits SDR), and FreeSync Premium Pro tricks. That’s enough to spell out where at least part of the extra $300 for this model is going, but I really want to capture the essence of what my eyeballs have enjoyed comparatively through testing.

I’ve spent enough time with IPS displays to know they just can’t keep up with OLED, and I’ve consistently felt underwhelmed with the ROG Xbox Ally X’s visuals compared to the Steam Deck OLED. Upon grabbing hold of the X20 for the first time, I sat upright on my bed in a dimly lit room in the exact same position I’d normally use its portable predecessor. If you want an embarrassing visual, picture me with my knees up, holding onto the pricey handheld like a steering wheel with my face far too close to the screen.

Sources indicate that as far as my senses were concerned, I was clutching a familiar portable. Little did I know that booting up Star Wars Galactic Racer would immediately signal that I wasn’t in IPS Kansas anymore, as seeing that Fuse logo ignite in sparks of yellow on what looked like an off display completely set my expectations for the visual experience ahead.

The peak brightness of the X20 alone is a fantastic achievement, as it pierces daylight and outshines even south-facing windows in my house. Glare has the potential to be an issue since we’re talking about a glossy screen, but I found that the elevated brightness, and the fact that you will block any direct light hitting the screen most of the time during play with your own presence, means it’s virtually negligible.

According to recent reports, I’ve argued on more than one occasion that vibrancy is often worth prioritising over other panel specs. Yes, playing games at 120Hz is lovely, and as I’ll get to, 1080p finally feels relevant in the portable realm thanks to chips like the Ryzen Z2 Extreme. But, I must admit that specs weren’t really on my mind while enjoying playing the MediEvil recomp over the spooky season, as the OLED screen fully pulled its weight in making the high-contrast PlayStation textures pop against the era-specific murky black short draw distances. Simply put, everything will look outstanding on this display, whether that means embracing HDR in Cyberpunk 2077 or messing with old PS1 romps.

Again, the X20 isn’t a sequel, and that means you’re not getting a generational revamp in terms of chip specs. On the AMD side of things, the Ryzen Z2 Extreme is as good as it gets for reasonable handhelds, and if you’re looking for a greater punch, you’ll either have to go for absurdly priced contenders by the likes of GPD WIN with a Ryzen AI MAX+ 395, or give Intel’s Arc G3 a try.

The real question you have to ask is whether you’re fine with paying $300 more to stick with virtually the same performance. It’s something I’ve been deliberating on while having an absolute blast playing games on the X20 at comparably lofty frame rates to the Steam Deck, and RAMageddon makes pointing price-point blame a little difficult. Still, there’s no getting around the fact that the same frame rate results for more money is a bad pitch, and it feels like this model exists to be an OLED fan crowd-pleaser.

In a recent development, benchmarking the same hardware 12 months later can normally lead to some funky results. It’s something that used to worry me in my early days as a hardware reviewer, as it’d gaslight me into thinking I’d messed up my original test run. In reality, it’s usually due to performance nuances between Windows updates, game patches, and various other factors that can hinder or help boost fps, so keep that in mind when looking at the ROG Xbox Ally X vs. X20.

In a recent development, for science, I’m running benchmarks on the Xbox Ally X20 anyway, as they can serve as updated Ryzen Z2 Extreme results. Spoiler: there are no real surprises in these stats, and driver updates seemingly haven’t given the AMD chipset any newfound muscle. If anything, I seem to have lost a few inconsequential frames, but that’s tied to the pain of gaming on Windows overall.

It has been revealed that kicking things off just like before with Cyberpunk 2077, and we’re working with a 52fps average at 1080p with everything cranked down low. That’s with no upscaling assistance, but it paints a performance picture without using tools like AMD FSR. I did manage to hit 54fps last time on the Xbox Ally X, so the X20 is hitting the same sub-60fps spot as before.

Recent findings suggest that that minor drop in comparative performance stands out a bit more in Total War: Warhammer 3, as for whatever reason, I lost around four frames compared to last time. I still hit 60fps in the RTS romp, even if only just, but it feels like something is happening under the Windows layers that’s preventing things from inching ahead compared to last time.

Weirdly, the trend continues with Shadow of the Tomb Raider, as I ended up with the same gap as with Cyberpunk 2077. It’s still within what I’d call a “margin of Windows fomfoolery”, as we’re talking 62fps vs 64 with the OG Xbox Ally X. I wouldn’t lose sleep over that difference, and chances are that it’s more just whatever the operating system is up to right now plus various other driver factors, but it draws a line under whether you’ll get higher performance via the OLED model.

In a recent development, since I’ve been spending so much time tearing up the track in a speeder, it feels only right to include Star Wars Galactic Racer in my benchmarking run this time around. If for no other reason, I wanted to include an example of a game that will run exceptionally well while still looking the part on “lower-end” hardware compared to your PC or home console. Considering the sci-fi death race just landed, I’m actually pretty staggered by the portable experience provided, and I’ll be using it as a test title going forward.

I really wouldn’t recommend dialling everything down to low at 1080p for Star Wars Galactic Racer, but if you’re not fussed about gnarly graphics, you’ll be treated to an 115fps average. At least, that’s the figure I got on Jakku during testing, but I opted to spend my leisure time playing with medium settings and AMD’s FSR bells and whistles enabled. That ended up producing visuals at a 70fps average that really looked on par with a console on a small screen, and even some of the funky effects of Frame Interpolation were easy to look past thanks to the elevated vibrancy and that 120Hz refresh rate.

Recent findings suggest that last year, the ROG Xbox Ally X arrived alongside Microsoft’s answer to SteamOS: Xbox Significant Screen Experience. It’s essentially an overlay for Windows 11, meant to ditch the notion that you’re using a bloated operating system primarily for desktop machines. I figured that over the span of twelve months, the Xbox-themed HUD would have evolved into something befitting of a next-gen console like Project Helix, but, uh, it feels like very little has changed.

Industry observers note that yes, micro upgrades have been pushed out, as Xbox Big Screen Experience now has a more fleshed-out Gamebar, optimized performance, and expanded compatibility with more portables. From a user perspective, though, all the irritating little bugs and quirks remain from last year, and in the instances where I did have a better time navigating the UI, it felt like I’d simply gotten more familiar with the overlay.

Here’s the thing: I quite like the Xbox Massive Screen Experience. At least, I find it preferable to going anywhere near Windows 11’s desktop. Jumping into games across almost every storefront is faster thanks to the carousel tab system, and getting a full view of your library in one place is a natural boon. Just don’t expect the Epic Games Store to remotely play nice on any of these portables, especially now that vibe coding has entered the scene (heads up: if you can’t access your library in Xbox Mode, adjust your desktop scaling).

I could write a whole article on Xbox Mode and all of its handheld hangups, including its tendency not to auto-switch to freshly opened applications, launch two instances of games like Cyberpunk 2077, and randomly decide to ignore the built-in controls. I might even still delve into all of that separately if I can, but my main takeaway is that it’s better than vanilla Windows 11. So long as you can brace yourself for a little bit of jank, you’ll have a cromulent console-inspired experience in your hands.

I’m hesitant to say the handheld PC scene hasn’t worked to resolve its glaring battery life problems. Asus specifically has been cramming chonkier 80Whr cells into its portables since before its Xbox partnership, and the new X20 model carries that baton with expected playtimes of around 3-4 hours in demanding romps.

In a recent development, the age-old catch of having to dial back screen brightness and wattage remains, though. Left to my own devices, I found that the X20 would putter out at around the two-hour mark, notably in games like Star Wars: Galactic Racer using 30W Turbo Mode. That’s longer than you’ll get out of some portables out there, particularly those that use traditional 40-50Wh cells while still pushing for higher wattages, but it’ll still result in you reaching for a high-wattage charger shortly into sessions.

It has been revealed that there are instances where you’ll absolutely get Switch 2 runtimes out of the Xbox Ally X20. For instance, I was able to get around 5 hours into my MediEvil Recomp playthrough before seeking a power source, which is a testament to efficiency. The Z2 Extreme itself also provides some headroom for messing around with settings and wattage to hit an experience that won’t tank your longevity, even if that does mean sacrificing 60fps in some scenarios.

I can’t hide my distaste for spending over $1,000 on any handheld gaming PC, given that the scene kickstarted with far cheaper contenders just a few years ago. It’s that price tag that ultimately prevents the ROG Xbox Ally X20 from soaring past its ever-so-slightly more affordable LCD sibling. However, its fabulous OLED panel and defined controls help the premium portable reach similar heights in my eyes, with the upgrades just about justifying the hikes for players who appreciate fancy perks.

That is to say that the ROG Xbox Ally X20 is one of the best gaming handhelds money can buy, but that doesn’t mean you should do just that. For some, this powerhouse will be a worthwhile investment that should be cheaper, but will deliver a notable on-the-go PC gaming experience in 2026. For others, it’s another princely portable that doesn’t offer enough of a revolutionary experience over older alternatives to be a viable option.

My regulars will be tired of reading this, but the gaming hardware scene, and I guess the world at large, is having a moment. Everything is inflated, costing more than it should and suffering through needlessly convoluted manufacturing circumstances that threaten the existence of consumer tech as a whole. In a way, the ROG Xbox Ally X20 is just another victim of RAMageddon, and that means while it’s objectively great, there are plenty of subjective reasons why you shouldn’t give in to paying more for it.

Sources indicate that over the course of a month, I used the ROG Xbox Ally X20 to benchmark a selection of test games while playing recent releases like Star Wars Galactic Racer in my spare time. Throughout testing, I assessed the portable's perceived and measurable performance while noting the overarching qualitative experience and physical feel of the device. In addition to playing contemporary games, I also made time to test projects like the MediEvil Recomp to get a feel for the device's low-end abilities side by side with its handling of major-budget releases using its Ryzen Z2 Extreme chipset.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this week sees the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, the open-world crime 'em up that's been in development for at least eight years and has been waited on by fans for even longer. Naturally, over on PC we're still waiting for a port to be announced, let alone a release date to circle in our calendars. But, as happens whenever a new GTA is on the horizon, I think about Mafia: City of Lost Heaven.

Released less than a year after Grand Theft Auto 3, Mafia is perhaps a more prescient example of Rockstar's future than their own.

Set in Lost Heaven, a shoe-in for 1930s Chicago, Illinois, you play through Tommy Angelo's rise from a taxi driver, who has a chance run in with the Salieri crime family, to one of the gang's main enforcers in their fight against their rivals, the Morellos.

It has been revealed that the influences on developers Illusion Softworks are obviously cinematic, with whole sequences ripped from The Godfather films and Goodfellas (and I'd argue there's a sprinkling of Once Upon A Time In America for good measure). A habit they share with Rockstar, who also pull liberally from crime films that share the settings of their games. But Illusion Softworks are also clearly interested in capturing the history of the Prohibition era, too. The story begins in the aftermath of the 1929 Wall Street Crash and the depression that followed, running through until the late 30s, and you see that time pass in the city around you. Buildings that are under construction at the start of the game are completed by its end, a used car lot in Chinatown sits empty for most of the game until business picks up with the economy, but most enjoyable of all is that the cars driving the streets change. At first the roads are filled with Ford Model-T-inspired vehicles that basically look like horse carriages with engines, but by the end of the game they've all become much sleeker creatures that have left their early carriage influences behind.

The city Illusion Softworks built also has a dedication to verisimilitude that we see Rockstar adopting in their later games. As you drive Lost Heaven's streets, you must pay attention to speed limits and red lights, as speeding and running traffic lights will both earn you a fine if a policeman spots you. For fans of public transport, there are streetcars and overhead trams you can ride to navigate the city, too. Two other touches I love: when you reload your gun, you dump the whole clip instead of returning the unfired bullets to a magic ammo reservoir, and vehicles can run out of fuel if you drive them too far.

Much had been made of all the simulations running under the surface of Grand Theft Auto 6, such as fully realised cloud formation, a smell reaction system, and… fuel tanks that can run empty. No doubt they're significantly more impressive than what's on show in Mafia, and this isn't about putting the two games against each other (even if one of them was likely made for less than the other studio spent on coffee runs across its eight-year development). Nor is it about saying history recognised the wrong game: Grand Theft Auto 3 was a huge step forward in open-world gaming and Mafia was recognised and celebrated in its time. It's about something else.

Back in 2002, Illusion Softworks offered a different kind of open-world crime game. One that was more mature despite having a lower age rating. Grand Theft Auto was undoubtedly more influential, sparking imitators that mostly opted to follow its tone and sensibilities – Saints Row began in a similar place to GTA 3 and as the series continued leaned further into the silliness and parody, for instance. But while for many years Mafia stood as a sign to an open world path that could have been taken, the longer Grand Theft Auto series has gone on, the more Rockstar have found their way toward the example set by Illusion Softworks. The games are still aiming for bombastic comedy at times, but they're also interested in the likes of newly-arrived-in-America Niko Belic, or Michael de Santa, a retired criminal haunted by his past. They're much richer protagonists than Claude, the silent character you play in GTA 3.

The Mafia series has continued, marked by ideas that remain as interesting as what was on show in the original. In Mafia 3, you play Lincoln Clay, a black soldier returned from the war in Vietnam and brought into the family. Set in a take on New Orleans, Louisiana, during the civil rights movement, you face overt racism. Linger too long in white, wealthy neighbourhoods and the residents will call on the police to move you along. And the Definitive Edition remake of the first game, released in 2020, is a rare example of a game that both captures the spirit of the original and justifies its existence by expanding and bettering the story. Though I don't think any of its sequels have been as innovative, nor as forward thinking, as the first game.

I don't want to come across as Rockstar-bashing. The studio have continued to push the open-world genre forward with every release and I want to see what other developers lift from GTA 6 for their own games. But I'm even more pleased that as the studio's aged, their work has grown closer to Illusion Softworks'.

It has been revealed that beats has a long history of making on-ear headphones that stand with the plushest and best-sounding cans on the market. As early Black Friday deals get underway, it's a great time to upgrade: Walmart has discounted the Beats Solo 4 by more than 65%, to $69 (originally $199.99); the sale applies to the Gray and Sandstone variants.

These headphones don’t have ANC, just passive isolation, but they still deliver solid sound, comfort, and strong battery life. They use physical controls and support one-touch pairing with most Apple devices, as well as hands-free Siri.A The Solo 4 headphones are compatible with Bluetooth 5.3 and work with the AAC and SBC codecs. They also support wired audio via 3.5mm or USB-C.

Sources indicate that the headphones last around 50 hours per charge (about 10 hours longer than their predecessor), and 10 minutes of charging gives you around five hours of playback, with a full recharge taking approximately two hours. In its review, PCMag describes the sound as “sculpted with accentuated bass and highs.".

Although they lack ANC and adjustable EQ, these headphones still have plenty of extra features for Apple users, and those shortcomings are much easier to forgive at almost 66% off. For $69, the Beats Solo 4 headphones are a compact and well-equipped option for casual listening, with long battery life and that classic Beats aesthetic.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft has stressed that its next-generation Xbox console, Project Helix, "is not a PC that can also play console games", but rather "a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC".
  • The details come from a Microsoft-produced Xbox magazine made available digitally yesterday, and a Helix-related feature speaking to Xbox vice president of next generation, Jason Ronald.
  • "We're very clear on the design goal," Ronald later added.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft has stressed that its next-generation Xbox console, Project Helix, "is not a PC that can also play console games", but rather "a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC". The tech giant has also underlined the importance of using gen-AI-adjacent "neural rendering" technology going forwards, and a desire to remove "all the barriers of play that have historically existed" - notably in making the past generations of games playable.

The details come from a Microsoft-produced Xbox magazine made available digitally yesterday, and a Helix-related feature speaking to Xbox vice president of next generation, Jason Ronald. "When we think about Project Helix, it's really designed to be the ultimate gaming machine," Ronald stated, "one that removes all the barriers of play that have historically existed. My entire library is accessible to me. I'm able to bring four generations of my Xbox library and progression with me and have it available instantly. And we remove the arbitrary constraints between console and PC games.

"We're very clear on the design goal," Ronald later added. "Helix is designed to be a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC. It is not a PC that can also play console games. The goal is making it easy, intuitive, and instant to access my games. But if you're a hardcore gamer or a power user who wants to have that deeper level of customisability across settings and performance options, you can absolutely go do it.".

It has been revealed that notably, Ronald seemed to suggest that Helix - the console, not the handheld; "Helix" refers to a couple of machines - isn't solely focused on computational grunt. Indeed, he noted the next generation wasn't about hitting 8K resolutions and 240 hertz frame-rates, but instead leaning on technologies like "neural rendering" - i.e. generative-AI - and encouraging innovation.

Recent findings suggest that "It's about deeper immersion," Ronald said. "It is about leveraging new technical advancements such as neural rendering to deliver a new level of visual fidelity in more efficient and innovative ways. It's about new kinds of games and new game experiences that we haven't been able to do before. What excites me about the future is the idea of entirely new types of games that have never been possible before, delivered through all the innovation in the silicon and the hardware and the platform that we're delivering.".

Sources indicate that while referencing the global component shortage and exorbitant prices of computer hardware, he added: "This is a big reason why we're really focused on advancements like neural rendering because it's an entirely upcoming way to generate a frame without requiring more computational horsepower, additional memory, and things like that. I think you're going to see more innovation over the next three to five years than you've seen in the last 10 years.".

Xbox boss Asha Sharma also recently talked up the importance of generative-AI-sounding technology in Xbox's future, saying "too many ideas never become games", and that "a single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations".

Another key part of Xbox's Helix vision is compatibility and game preservation. "Game preservation is core to Xbox," Ronald went as far as to say. "Not only do we feel like it's the right thing for the industry, we feel a deep responsibility as one of its biggest platforms and publishers. For the first 30 years of game development, nobody really thought about game preservation when they were designing their hardware, when they were building their games." Xbox is apparently working with game-makers to ensure games can not only be played now but also 20 to 30 years into the future.

Sources indicate that the other key facet of Microsoft's push the familiar Play Anywhere mantra, whereby one game can be played across multiple devices, maintaining your game-progress as you go. This is fundamental to Microsoft's handheld-and-console Helix plan, and something we've seen the company dry-run with the Xbox ROG Ally X handheld. "It's this notion that not only does my library move with me, but my progress moves with me as well," Ronald mentioned. "Because I fully expect that when I'm in the middle of an 80-hour RPG, if I'm 25 hours into that and I want to play it on another device, I should be able to instantly resume from where I was. Those are things that today are becoming more common, but I think in the future it's going to be a baseline expectation of all players.".

Ronald wouldn't be drawn on the matter of price regarding Project Helix - a recent report suggested Helix could be priced up to $1800 - referring to it only as both "a challenging time" but an "exciting one", because "we have to invent entirely new technology to continue to advance the state-of-the-art while also continuing to make things accessible and affordable". Ronald also wouldn't reference a release date, though the report referenced above suggested the handheld Helix machine will release next holiday, 2027, and the console Helix machine the year after. The next generation, then, seems to be around the corner.

#166300. My murderous wine merchant whines for a chance at republican rule in Crusader Kings 3’s Silk and Silver expansion, which isn't only about the money

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2080 w)

My murderous wine merchant whines for a chance at republican rule in Crusader Kings 3’s Silk and Silver expansion, which isn't only about the money

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2080 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The tentacles of my trade empire snake up towards France in the west, down towards Africa in the south, and off into Hungary in the east.
  • According to recent reports, I’ve shed blood in its name, the blood of someone else named Marco no less.
  • Sources indicate that it should, in theory, help that he’s my best mate, thanks to a well-timed feast.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The tentacles of my trade empire snake up towards France in the west, down towards Africa in the south, and off into Hungary in the east. Yet, I still can’t reach out and grasp the throne that sits right in front of me. I’m Marco Sanudo, and the throne of the serene republic of Venice eludes me.

According to recent reports, I’ve shed blood in its name, the blood of someone else named Marco no less. I’ve managed to avoid punishment for that crime, despite the fact it earned me a fiefdom to rule while I’ve tried to up my patrician score enough to be the lucky party the next time a ruling Doge dies in office (or runs out their 10 year term). Sadly, Doge Leonardo, the mysterious masked lord who’s had an iron grip on power since the first couple of old blokes to hold the position in this playthrough popped their clogs, is proving incredibly tough to oust.

Sources indicate that it should, in theory, help that he’s my best mate, thanks to a well-timed feast. It certainly did in being granted a pardon for offing that other Marco, but not even that and a plague which infected nearly everyone in the realm aside from me have paved the way to Dogedom. In the meantime, I’ve striven to gain wealth and influence. I’ve worked up to having four trade routes running at once, with goods like wine, iron, and textiles flowing from market to market across southern Europe and bringing a steady supply of coin back to my Venetian estate. I’ve built trade posts at the extremities of my routes, giving me the option of starting from further afield and reaching new lands if the cash flow dries up closer to home.

This is where Crusader Kings 3’s Silk and Silver expansion has blended a bit with the game’s traditional feudal moneymaking to supercharge my coffers. The land holding I killed a dude for, the Proveditorate of Zara, means I’ve also had tax money from modern day Croatia to add to both my trade profits and the income my domicile generates on its own. I am, as the medieval kids say, minted.

Getting to the point of serious pocket clinkage is, as you might imagine given Silk and Silver’s focus on filling the game’s world with travelling merchant companies and wheeler-dealing republican patrician families, the beating heart of the expansion. A near-constant stream of notifications about prices of different goods I’m trying to hawk in different locations encourage me to regularly prune and re-work my routes so that max profits are being earned and no carrying capacity’s being wasted. The bubbling up of wars and plagues impacts prices in affected cities, making it a never-ending battle if you’re desperate to optimise everything within an inch of its life. I’ve found that degree of micromanagement unnecessary if the goal is just to keep a decent profit margin ticking over. Just remember to replace the trader assigned to a route if they die, recall them every few years so they don’t stress themselves to death, and check in every so often to re-evaluate whether you’re running goods that are suitably in demand.

If you stick at it for a decent amount of time, with a certain type of good - alcohol or jewellery, for example - your expertise in dealing in them increases, making it easier to sell for better prices. Trade routes left running between the same markets also gain boons from being in place for a long time, offering a counterpoint to rejigging them every five seconds to wring out a few more coins. Most of my routes have run along a path that includes stops at four markets, with the occasional location boasting a monopoly I’ve bargained for with the local ruler, so I don’t have to worry about competition at every stop.

When you’re playing as a merchant who isn’t locked into the ruling inner circle of a republic, making your routes as lengthy as possible is one of the three moneymaking areas your company can specialise in. That first one’s caravaneering, and is the one I leant into in a non-Marco Sanudo playthrough. Beyond that, you can become an expert loan shark, lending cash to rulers or paying their ransoms in order to recoup interest and collect hooks you can use for favours. Manufacturing expensive artifacts that can be sold individually to collectors for a profit is the third option. The latter two I’ve only dabbled in a little bit as of writing, having earned enough gold mostly from caravanneering to buy the land containing the city with my home market and be anointed a Sheikh. So, beginning as a landless merchant is a nice alternative to Crusader Kings 3’s long-established wandering adventurer starting point, with both allowing you to work your way up from lowly serf to landed lordly dynasty in your location of choice.

In a recent development, if you’re after a more specific historical scenario, Silk and Silver has Guelphs and Ghibellines. This is where we find Marco Sanudo, as well as the other patrician family head I’ve played as thus far, Speronella Dalesmanni. The setup is that the Pope and the Holy Roman Emperor have had a bit of a tiff, essentially rooted in who should have certain powers, with different cities and powerful families in northern Italy taking either the Guelph (Pope-likers) or Ghibelline (Holy Roman Empire-enjoyers) side depending on what suits their goals or principles. I’ll be honest, aside from being another way to easily earn friends or enemies in the ruthless crucible of merchant republican politics, where votes and reputation-bolstering aid from other nobles are key, the situation’s not had a hugely obvious bearing on my playthroughs thus far.

Industry observers note that I think the closest it’s come is during my Dalesmanni run, if largely due to the existence of the By God Alone expansion allowing a newly introduced branch of Catholicism, dubbed Italian Christianity, to be created. The initial conversion push from the bishop responsible led a number of my fellow northern Italian nobles away from the Roman Rite headed by his Popeliness, making the Guelph/Ghibelline split more clearly defined.

In the early hours of both my Sanudo and Dalesmanni playthroughs, I’ve been far more focused on simply trying to push the respective patrician families up the hill from posh toffs with naught but a vote and a manor to elected rulers of their great cities, with land holdings to match. Speronella’s situation in Padua is made incredibly tough by the fact she’s a woman in a world where every succession rule is designed to put blokes first, so I’ve had more success with Marco and his quest to become the Doge of Venice.

As the head of a patrician family, one of select few elite clans who steer the oligarchical republic, I was faced with earning Marco enough respect among his fellow family heads that they’d consider voting him to the top of the succession list, thus securing his power whenever the current Doge got the boot. Pulling that off, while also not kowtowing to the requests and schemes of those same peers, isn’t easy. A large cocktail of factors go into determining whether another noble likes you enough to vote in support of your succession. There’s your patrician rating, which is upped by doing things which specifically show you to be good at this Italian noble house lark, such as establishing trade monopolies for the republic, gaining the Pope’s favour, or having close relatives who also hold key positions in the republic. However, how close a friendship you have with the target and how their character traits align with you also play a huge rule.

Sources indicate that thus it was that, at one point, Marco was best mates with the current Doge and had a decent patrician rating, but had only amassed 68 of the 72 points needed for mentioned Doge to vote for him because the Doge was generous, and therefore didn’t care for Marco’s ambitiousness. That same Doge either liked or respected Marco enough to grant him a council position and the status of regent, but he would not back Marco to replace him permanently for love nor money. This is the same man who liked Marco so much that when I pulled off that not-so-sneaky murder on another noble house head in order to inherit the keys to the Proveditorate of Zara, the Doge was instantly willing to pardon me and prevent Marco suffering any punishment for the crime.

Industry observers note that not even a couple of serious plagues hitting Venice, which at one point had all three people ahead of Marco in the queue suffering from smallpox, could get him on that throne. Eventually, it took a bit of lucky timing when his Doge mate died of old age - a few years after beating smallpox - to finally install Marco as Doge. Given that delayed promotion, as of writing I’ve not yet had enough time in the big chair to give a proper verdict on how it differs from regular feudal rulerdom in the long run.

According to recent reports, what I can do instead is tell you a bit about the fun of council votes. The same pool of voters who in a republic like Venice, get a say in who succeeds the ruler, also vote on the passage of laws and decrees. One proposal you can put forward is a vote to change who exactly is allowed a seat in this voting pool. It defaults to just being heads of patrician families, but can be extended to include all vassals, or tightened up so only the Doge’s councillors or the ruler themselves have a say, that being the way despotism lies. As you can imagine, passing a change to who can vote can drastically change the state of play, either tightening up the number of folks who might oppose or support you, or bringing latest folks into play in a fashion that dilutes individual power, but gives you more pieces on the board to mind or manipulate to your advantage.

In a recent development, I’ve found it suitably tough to orchestrate successful votes to change laws and customs which medieval Italian noble families, expectedly, have firmly entrenched stances on. Getting rid of checks and balances, such as the requirement to vote on banishments or wars - so the Doge can rule as a despot - has proven one such challenge, as has changing laws governing men being prioritised over women. I tried to pass equal succession as a substitute for men being put first while playing as Speronella, but met an insurmountable wall of resistance due to the region’s culture and faith. So, all I could do was try to put my young male heir in the best position possible to make the sorts of gains I couldn’t.

Sources indicate that much easier to weasel into place, either through some canny swaying or the offering of hooks, are laws giving state backing or other priority to trading in certain types of goods. Alcohol, for instance, which certainly hasn’t hurt the profits of Marco’s two wine trade routes.

Thus, cash continues to flow through the tentacles of my trade empire in sizable globs. As he’s now Doge, I’ve got Marco using the ample funds of Venice’s treasury to build a latest piazza and have him focused on making the city’s already-strong trade league even more formidable, by attracting new members from the few other northern Italian blocs.

While I’m fairly sure there are folks who’ll find Silk and Silver's constant barrage of trade route notifications annoying, or that their power-grabbing skills and sheer multitude of money-making means combine to make playthroughs less challenging than they could be, so far I've found it another enjoyably sonorous string to Crusader Kings 3’s bow. Above all else, playing as a merchant gives more reason to invest in stewardship skills beyond just maximising your tax yields, while the republican politics of the DLC's main region fleshes out rewarding intrigue-focused builds. Diplomacy and martial skills are less key, but still have their place at times.

If you’re an absolute stickler for historical accuracy, you may well find other things to gripe about, but aside from the Guelph and Ghibelline conflict fading into the background, I’ve found plenty to like in my quest to become top Doge.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

James Lowder, a freelance writer and editor who has contracted with Wizards of the Coast on D&D books, discussed the news and its personal impact on him via LinkedIn. Here's the second half of Lowder's post, explaining the mechanics of how this came about:.

Industry observers note that "This is remarkable and amounts to hundreds of thousands of dollars that WotC could have collected going to the writers. And Wizards is doing this at a time when the larger publishers are scrambling to grab as much settlement money as possible from authors. Amazing. This payout will help a lot of writers--folks who certainly deserve to be rewarded for their work.

In a recent development, "Conversations at Wizards about the Anthropic settlement have been ongoing for months. (I've been part of these conversations on and off, but the real heavy lifting was done by folks with more clout.) This all came about because some of the writers used what influence they possessed to raise the concern and because the people inside Wizards, up to the highest levels, were willing to consider the situation from more than a financial perspective.

It has been revealed that "Thanks to all the writers who stepped up here. I don't think this would have happened without those author-prompted discussions, especially the efforts of R.A. Salvatore. Huge credit to the folks at Wizards, in particular Dan Ayoub, who were open to the discussions and then did the generous (and right) thing here. And it was the right thing to do.".

Recent findings suggest that it is unambiguously great that writers like Lowder benefitted from this settlement more than they were required to⁠—it's the spiritual opposite of all the companies that pocketed their tariff refunds instead of passing them onto the consumers who ate inflated prices. The authors who make D&D great deserve it. You do gotta hand it to Wizards.

But. In the interest of providing full context, I have to be a cynical prick for the remainder of this article. Wizards of the Coast's reputation has taken a drubbing in recent years, and even though D&D and Magic are practically synonymous with tabletop and TCGs respectively, it behooves the tech giant to secure PR victories like this where it can.

According to recent reports, most recently, Wizards has refused to voluntarily recognize an employee union twice in one year, forcing a vote among the staff. The results of the ballot are not yet public, but Wargamer reported last week that the company appears to be preparing to deal with a unionised workforce.

Recent findings suggest that moving back in time, Wizards' attempt to rework D&D's influential Open Gaming License (OGL) met a huge fan and industry backlash, prompting the company to backpedal almost immediately. Contemporaneously, incidents of AI art appearing in marketing material and a D&D sourcebook similarly met with a sour response.

In a recent development, and the whopper: Wizards of the Coast laid off 1,100 people in 2023, including much of the publishing team that liaised with Larian Studios on Baldur's Gate 3. Larian has insisted that its decision to pivot from D&D back to its own Divinity series was a creative one, and that its shift away from Wizards was amicable, but most forum-goers and hoi polloi still assume the worst about the split.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We all know the story of GTA 5 making more than $1 billion in the first three days it was on sale, right?
  • At least, that's according to one analyst, Joost van Dreunen, a senior data analyst and great writer/numbers diviner who wrote some predictions in his respected SuperJoost PlayList newsletter.
  • Let's review what we already know: there is a conservative estimate of 10 million pre-orders for Rockstar's latest game floating around - something buoyed by comments from Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick - and, even by the firm's lofty expectations, we know the game is tracking "well above expectations" when it comes to pre-orders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We all know the story of GTA 5 making more than $1 billion in the first three days it was on sale, right? At the time, Take-Two believed this to be the fastest any entertainment property had achieved the impressive milestone - music and films included. It made history, and with ease. And it looks like GTA 6 is going to do even better.

At least, that's according to one analyst, Joost van Dreunen, a senior data analyst and great writer/numbers diviner who wrote some predictions in his respected SuperJoost PlayList newsletter. "My prediction: Take-Two unveils opening-weekend sales above $2 billion by Monday, 23rd November," he wrote. And you know what? I reckon he's onto something.

Let's review what we already know: there is a conservative estimate of 10 million pre-orders for Rockstar's latest game floating around - something buoyed by comments from Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick - and, even by the firm's lofty expectations, we know the game is tracking "well above expectations" when it comes to pre-orders.

Recent findings suggest that we also know a lot of people are shelling out for the slightly more pricey Ultimate Edition (£90). So many people are opting for the more expensive version, in fact, that Take-Two revised its financial forecast up to $3.5bn for the next financial quarter, thanks to "recurrent consumer spending" (something Zelnick clarified in an investor's call is explicitly linked to the Ultimate Edition). 10 million pre-orders, at roughly $100 per copy - that's $1 billion right off the bat.

Industry observers note that "That’s two days faster than its predecessor," van Dreunen noted, "and largely before anyone has even played the game." That other $1bn will come over the weekend. And then, per the analyst, the game will sell roughly another 28 million copies over the course of the first year it's on sale. "My forecast puts first-year sales at 38 million copies, only modestly ahead of GTA 5’s 35 million. The real difference may be how much revenue each player generates over the years that follow.".

Sources indicate that but it's what follows in the newsletter that intrigues me most. "At the high end, [GTA 6] may just lift the entire industry with it," wrote van Dreunen. "In the face of AI slop and shitty mobile games that exist only to extract revenue, it will offer a reprieve. At a time when the industry is increasingly focused on making games cheaper and monetising players more aggressively, Rockstar is about to demonstrate the enduring appeal of spending a fortune to make something people actually want to play.".

So, even if you're dubious about the game and Rockstar's motivations for selling as many copies as possible, the launch of GTA 6 could be something that gives the industry a much-needed jolt of life, in the face of rampant layoffs and shrinking talent pools.

It's not all sunshine and rainbows ahead for Rockstar, though: amongst the frenzy of launch activity, Rockstar has been embroiled in legal action after it was accused of union busting following the firing of over 30 employees. The case's conclusion will be determined this week, as the game goes on sale.

💡 Key Takeaways
